items.t: Caltrans Standard Specifications: structure and how to read them
items.s: What the Standard Specifications are, how they are organized, and how a project manager actually uses them on an electrical contract.
items.x: Caltrans Standard Specifications: structure and how to read them In one sentence: the Standard Specifications are the rulebook that applies to every Caltrans contract. They tell you how work must be done, what materials are acceptable, how it is measured and how you get paid. .") What they are Caltrans publishes the Standard Specifications as one large book that is updated every few years. Every contract you bid on names the edition that applies, and that edition is part of the contract — even though it is not printed in your bid package. The Standard Specifications are generic : they are written for every highway project in the state. What makes them specific to your job is the combination with: the special provisions , which modify and add to the specs for this project, the project plans , which show what to build and where, the standard plans es , which show standard details (pull boxes, foundations, conduit installation). When these documents disagree, a defined order of precedence decides which one wins. How the book is organized The specifications are divided into divisions , and each division into numbered sections . A reference such as 86 2.05 reads as Section 86, subsection 2, paragraph 05 . Part What it covers Why it matters to an electrical PM Sections 1–9 — General provisions Definitions, bidding, award, scope, control of work, legal relations, prosecution and progress, payment Submittals, schedule, change orders, payment and claims all live here Sections 10–16 — General construction Work zone and traffic control, water pollution control, environmental stewardship, existing facilities Every freeway job: lane closures, BMPs during trenching, protecting existing equipment Earthwork, concrete, paving sections Excavation and backfill, concrete, asphalt and concrete repair Trench backfill, foundations, pull box surrounds, patching after trenching Section 86 — Electrical systems (general) Requirements common to all electrical work: conduit, pull boxes, conductors, splicing, grounding, service, foundations, testing The section you will open most often Section 87 — Electrical systems (specific) Each system: signals, lighting, detection, ramp metering, traffic monitoring, communications, fiber optics Where system specific materials and tests are defined Section numbers follow the recent editions of the book. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract. Anatomy of a section Most sections follow the same pattern. Once you know it, you can find anything quickly: 1. General — scope, definitions, submittals required, quality control. 2. Materials — what is acceptable (standards, ratings, approved products). 3. Construction — how to install it. 4. Payment — how the item is measured and paid (per linear foot, each, lump sum). For a PM, the two parts you read first are Submittals (what you must send before ordering or installing) and Payment (what you are actually paid for, and what is included in another item at no extra cost). How a PM uses them day to day Bidding: read the payment clause for each bid item so you know what is included in the price — for example, whether trenching and backfill are paid separately or included in the conduit item. Preconstruction: list every submittal the relevant sections require and build the submittal log from it. See submittals. Procurement: check the Materials subsections before you request quotes, so the supplier quotes a product that will be approved. See procurement long lead. In the field: when the crew asks "how deep?" or "what backfill?", the answer is in the Construction subsection — unless the special provisions or plans say otherwise. Testing and closeout: the required tests and documentation are listed in the sections; they become your acceptance checklist. See acceptance testing punch list. The rule that saves the most trouble Never read the Standard Specifications alone. Before relying on any clause, check whether the special provisions for your project modify it. Many

items.t: Project lifecycle: the twelve phases of a Caltrans electrical job
items.s: The order a Caltrans electrical project runs in, from design review to turnover, and what the PM does in each phase.
items.x: In one sentence: a job moves from paper to pipe to wire to equipment to tests, and each phase depends on the one before it. The flow Design review → RFIs → submittals → procurement → underground conduit → pull boxes → foundations → poles and cabinets → conductors and fiber → equipment → configuration → testing → Caltrans acceptance → punch list → closeout. Phase What happens PM focus 1. phase 1 preconstruction Read the contract, find conflicts, submit, order long lead items Submittals, RFIs, baseline schedule 2. phase 2 underground Survey, potholing, trenching or boring, conduit Utility conflicts, lane closures 3. phase 3 pull boxes foundations Pull boxes, vaults, cabinet and pole foundations Inspections before concrete 4. phase 4 structures Poles, cabinets, solar assemblies Deliveries arriving in order 5. phase 5 cable installation Conductors, fiber and communication cable Conduit proven clear first 6. phase 6 equipment installation Switches, routers, cameras, power equipment Approved equipment only 7. phase 7 fiber splicing Fusion splicing, termination, fiber tests Splice plan and test records 8. phase 8 network configuration IP addresses, VLANs, remote access Caltrans network requirements 9. phase 9 system testing Electrical, communication and functional tests Test reports 10. phase 10 acceptance testing Caltrans witnesses tests Scheduling with the RE 11. phase 11 punch list Fix every deficiency Closing items fast 12. phase 12 closeout As builts, certificates, warranties, final quantities Getting paid in full How procurement runs through it Procurement isn't a phase; it runs alongside all of them. Long lead equipment ordered in phase 1 has to arrive in phases 4 to 6. Late equipment is the most common reason an electrical job finishes late. See procurement long lead. Four systems, one job Everything you order supports one of four systems: civil (conduit, concrete, pull boxes), electrical (conductors, breakers, grounding), communications (fiber, cable, switches, routers) and power (utility service, or solar and batteries).

items.s: The protected pathway for power and communication cables: conduit types, fittings, and what a PM checks when ordering and installing it.
items.x: In one sentence: conduit is the empty pipe that protects every conductor and fiber on the job, and it is usually the largest quantity you install. Types The specifications name the conduit allowed for each use. In general terms: Rigid non metallic (PVC), Schedule 40 or 80: the usual choice underground. Rigid steel (galvanized): where more protection is needed, such as exposed runs, structures and some crossings. Coated rigid steel and flexible conduit for specific locations, as the specifications and plans allow. Which type goes where comes from Section 86, the special provisions and the plans. Sizes are shown on the plans or the conduit schedule. Materials ordered with it Item What it is for Elbows (22.5°, 45°, 90°) Change direction; sweep radius matters for fiber Couplings Join conduit sections Expansion fittings Let conduit move with temperature, for example on bridges Bell ends and bushings Protect cables where conduit enters a box Pull tape (mule tape) Left in the conduit to pull cable later. See pull tape tracer wire warning tape Innerduct Subdivides a conduit for fiber Sand bedding, slurry or concrete Bedding and encasement as specified Installation notes Depth, slope and bedding follow Section 86 and the plans. Keep runs clean: cap open ends during work. Prove each run clear (mandrel or swab) before cables are pulled, and when the contract requires it, before it is buried. Leave pull tape in every empty conduit. PM notes Conduit is often paid by the linear foot by size and type. Keep good daily records of footage installed; final quantities come from them. See daily reports.

items.t: How a Caltrans electrical bid comes together
items.s: From the weekly ad to the bid opening: the steps, who does what, and how many weeks you really have to build an electrical estimate.
items.x: In one sentence: a Caltrans electrical bid is a few weeks of work squeezed between the ad and the bid opening: read the package, take off quantities, price labor, material, equipment and subs, check it, and submit it electronically. The steps 1. Decide whether to bid. Scope, location, size, schedule, risk, your workload. See when to pass on a job. 2. Get the package: plans, special provisions, Bid Item List, addenda. See bid package. 3. Read it and list questions and risks. See reading the bid item list. 4. Take off quantities from the plans. See electrical takeoff. 5. Price labor from crew productivity. See pricing electrical labor. 6. Get material quotes. See material quotes electrical. 7. Price equipment and indirect costs. See equipment and indirect costs. 8. Collect subcontractor quotes and plan bid day. See sub quotes and bid day. 9. Check the bid before it goes. See checking your bid. 10. Submit electronically before the deadline, then learn from the results. See after the bid. How much time you have Caltrans says its projects are advertised for three to seven weeks, and bids can be submitted and resubmitted any time before the bid opening. Plan backwards from the opening: takeoff in the first third, quotes requested by the middle, bid day reserved for numbers that arrive late. Electronic bidding Caltrans major contracts are bid electronically with its bidding software and an online bidding service. First time bidders need a Bidder ID and a digital ID; Caltrans advises allowing at least 7 days to finish registration. Do it before you need it. Who does what in a small company Task Usually Bid/no bid, final price Owner Takeoff and labor pricing Estimator or PM Material and sub quotes Estimator, with the office Bid forms, bonds, DBE and sub listing Office, checked by the owner PM notes Every estimate becomes the job's budget. Organize it by the same cost codes you'll use to track the job. See job costing. Official sources Caltrans Office Engineer: Bidder's Guide · Electronic bidding.

items.s: Reading the contract, finding conflicts, submitting, ordering long-lead items and building the schedule before any field work.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 1 is where you win or lose the schedule: everything you don't catch on paper now becomes a delay in the field later. What happens Review the contract: special provisions, project plans and standard plans es side by side. List every piece of equipment and every test. Find conflicts: utilities, right of way, drainage, existing electrical facilities, and conflicts between documents. Send RFIs early. See rfis. Baseline CPM schedule: the schedule Caltrans approves and measures you against. First submittals: traffic control plans, the water pollution control program, shop drawings and material submittals. See submittals. Order long lead items: cabinets, batteries, routers, switches, fiber components, poles. See procurement long lead. Preconstruction meeting with the Resident Engineer: contacts, working hours, lane closure process, submittal routing. PM checklist 1. Submittal log built from the specifications. 2. Long lead list with supplier quotes and lead times. 3. RFI log started. 4. Schedule with procurement activities, not only field work. 5. Existing facility conflicts walked in the field, with photos. Goal: approvals in hand and material on order before the crew needs them.

items.t: Special Provisions: what they change and why they win
items.s: What the Special Provisions are, how they relate to the Standard Specifications, and how a project manager reads them on a Caltrans electrical job.
items.x: Special Provisions: what they change and why they win In one sentence: the Special Provisions are the part of the contract written for this project. They change, delete and add to the standard specifications, and when the two disagree, the Special Provisions govern. .") Where they fit Every Caltrans contract is built from the same rulebook, the Standard Specifications, plus documents written for the job. The Special Provisions are the most important of those project documents. They arrive in the bid package (in the Notice to Bidders and Special Provisions book), together with the project plans and the bid forms. Together, the Special Provisions, the Revised Standard Specifications and the Standard Specifications make up the contract specifications . You never read one without the others. What is inside Special Provisions are organized with the same section numbers as the Standard Specifications, so Section 86 of the Special Provisions talks about the same subject as Section 86 of the book. Inside, you will typically find: Replacements: a paragraph of the Standard Specifications is replaced with new wording. Additions: new paragraphs or new subsections, for work the book doesn't cover or covers differently. Deletions: a requirement of the book that doesn't apply to this job. Project specific information: working days, liquidated damages, the DBE goal, the edition of the Standard Specifications and Standard Plans that applies, and any Revised Standard Plans. Most of the text is not written from scratch. Caltrans maintains Standard Special Provisions (SSPs) , standard wording that designers pick and fill in. When no standard wording fits, the designer writes a non standard special provision (nSSP) . On electrical jobs, the nSSPs are where you usually find specific equipment: a particular cabinet, router, switch, camera or battery requirement. How a PM uses them At bid time: read Sections 86 and 87 of the Special Provisions before pricing anything. Approved products, testing requirements and payment rules often change there. For submittals: every "submit" in the Special Provisions adds a line to your submittal log, on top of what the Standard Specifications already require. See submittals. For procurement: an nSSP that names a specific product or performance requirement is a long lead warning. Ask suppliers early. See procurement long lead. In the field: when the crew's question is answered by the book, check that the Special Provisions don't say otherwise before giving the answer. Why they win The contract sets an order of precedence for when its parts disagree, and the Special Provisions sit at the top of it: they govern over the project plans, the Standard Specifications and the Standard Plans. That is why the rule "never read the Standard Specifications alone" matters so much. If the conflict is real and the order of precedence doesn't settle it, don't guess: send an RFI to the Resident Engineer and wait for a written answer. Section numbers and document names follow recent editions. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract.

items.s: The parts of a Caltrans traffic signal system, from the controller cabinet to the heads and push buttons, and how a job installs them.
items.x: In one sentence: a traffic signal is a controller in a cabinet that switches signal heads in a timed sequence, adjusted by what the detectors see. Main parts Part What it does Controller and cabinet Runs the timing; Caltrans uses standard controller and cabinet models named in the contract. See equipment cabinets Signal standards and mast arms Hold the heads over and beside the road. See foundations Signal heads Vehicle and pedestrian indications, usually LED Pedestrian push buttons Call a pedestrian phase; accessible push buttons where required Detection Tells the controller where vehicles are. See vehicle detection Emergency vehicle preemption Gives emergency vehicles a green, when specified Battery backup Keeps the signal running in a power outage. See battery backup systems Signal and interconnect cable From cabinet to heads, and to other signals or the TMC Details are on the ES standard plans es and the signal sheets of the plans. How it is built Conduit and pull boxes, foundations, standards and cabinet, cable, heads and buttons, then cabinet wiring and the turn on. Turn on A new or modified signal is turned on in a planned sequence agreed with Caltrans: timing loaded, heads checked, often with temporary traffic control and Caltrans staff present. PM notes Signal work at an existing intersection is often staged to keep the signal running. Plan temporary signals or staging. Order the controller cabinet early; it may need factory testing.

items.t: What a Caltrans electrical contractor does
items.s: The work an electrical contractor builds along California highways, who it works for, and how a job is organized.
items.x: In one sentence: an electrical contractor on a Caltrans job builds the power, communications and field devices that let Caltrans light, signal, watch and manage the highway. The work Most Caltrans electrical work falls into a few families of systems: Traffic signals at ramps and intersections. See traffic signals. Vehicle detection that counts and measures traffic. See vehicle detection. Highway lighting and sign lighting. See highway lighting. Ramp metering , the signals that release cars onto the freeway. See ramp metering. Traffic monitoring and ITS : cameras, changeable message signs and the stations that report to the Traffic Management Center. See cctv and video and changeable message signs. Communications that tie it all together: fiber optics, network switches and cellular routers. See fiber optic communications and network equipment. Power for all of it, from a utility service or, at remote sites, from solar panels and batteries. See service equipment and solar power and batteries. Underneath every system is the same civil work: conduit, pull boxes and foundations. That is usually most of the crew's hours. Who is who Caltrans is the owner. On each contract, a Resident Engineer (RE) runs the job for Caltrans, with inspectors in the field. The prime contractor holds the contract. On an electrical only job, the electrical contractor is often the prime; on a larger job (paving, bridges), it is usually a subcontractor to the prime. Suppliers furnish the materials and equipment, and specialty subcontractors may handle fiber splicing, boring or striping. How a job is organized Every job follows the same arc: read the contract, get submittals approved, order material, build underground, install structures and equipment, test, get Caltrans to accept it, and close out. The lifecycle overview walks through the twelve phases. The contract itself is a set of documents: the standard specifications, the special provisions, the project plans and the standard plans es. Knowing how to read them, and which one wins, is half the job. See order of precedence.

items.s: How to write a Request for Information that gets a fast, clear answer from the Resident Engineer.
items.x: In one sentence: an RFI is a written question to the engineer when the contract is unclear, contradictory, or doesn't match the field. When to write one Two documents disagree and the order of precedence doesn't settle it. A requirement is unclear or missing. The field doesn't match the plans: a utility in the way, a grade that doesn't work, an existing facility not shown. What a good RFI contains 1. A clear subject: location and topic, for example "Pull box at Sta 12+50: conflict with storm drain". 2. References: sheet numbers, specification sections, photos. 3. The problem , stated in one or two sentences. 4. A proposed solution. It speeds the answer and shows you've thought about it. 5. The impact: what is on hold, and by when you need an answer. One question per RFI. Number them and keep a log: number, date sent, subject, date answered, answer, and whether it affects cost or time. After the answer If the answer changes the work, cost or time, it may lead to a change order. Say so in writing quickly. See change orders. PM notes Send RFIs early. One sent in phase 1 costs a day; one found in the field costs a crew.

items.t: Order of precedence: which contract document wins
items.s: When the Special Provisions, plans, Standard Specifications and Standard Plans disagree, Section 5-1.02 decides which one governs. Here is the order and how to use it.
items.x: Order of precedence: which contract document wins In one sentence: when two parts of a Caltrans contract disagree, Section 5 1.02 of the standard specifications lists which one governs, starting with the special provisions. .") The order Section 5 1.02 ( Contract Components , in Section 5, Control of Work ) lists the parts of the contract in the order they govern when there is a discrepancy: 1. Special Provisions 2. Project plans 3. Standard Specifications (as revised by the Revised Standard Specifications) 4. Revised Standard Plans 5. Standard Plans 6. Supplemental project information The same section adds one more rule: on a drawing, written numbers and notes govern over the graphics . If a dimension is written on the plan, use it; don't scale the drawing. What it means in practice Special Provisions over everything: if the Special Provisions call for a different pull box, conductor or test than the plans or the book, follow the Special Provisions. Project plans over the book and the Standard Plans: the plans show this job. If a detail on the project plans differs from the Standard Plan it refers to, the project plan wins. Revised Standard Plans over Standard Plans: when a Standard Plan sheet has been revised since the edition you are using, the revised sheet is included with the contract and replaces it. Supplemental project information last: reports and reference material (for example, geotechnical or utility information) inform the work but don't override the contract requirements above it. When the order isn't enough The order of precedence settles conflicts between documents. It doesn't settle: a requirement that is unclear rather than contradictory, a conflict inside one document, a conflict between the documents and what you find in the field (a utility where the conduit should go, a foundation that doesn't fit). In those cases, write an RFI to the Resident Engineer, describe the conflict with sheet and section references, and propose a solution. Keep working on what isn't affected, and don't build the disputed item until you have a written answer: work done on a guess may not be paid. A quick check before you build 1. Find the requirement in the Special Provisions (same section number as the book). 2. Check the project plans and their notes. 3. Check the Standard Specifications and any Revised Standard Specifications. 4. Check the Revised Standard Plans, then the Standard Plans. 5. Still unclear? RFI. Based on Section 5 1.02 of recent editions. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract.

items.s: Survey and staking, potholing, then trenching or directional boring to install the conduit pathway.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 2 builds the empty pathway every future system will use, and it is where most surprises are found. What happens Survey and staking: mark pull boxes, poles, cabinets and conduit routes from the plans. Utility locates: call the one call center before digging, and wait for marks. Potholing: expose existing utilities where the route crosses or runs close to them. Confirm depth and owner. If a conflict appears, stop and write an RFI; it may become a change order. See change orders. Trenching or directional boring: install conduit, innerduct and any ground or tracer wire. See trenching vs boring and conduit. Backfill and restoration to the specification, then patch paving. PM focus Lane closures booked and traffic control set up as approved. Water pollution control BMPs in place before digging. Daily reports that record what was found, especially utility conflicts and delays. See daily reports. Conduit proven clear (mandrel or swab) before it is covered when the contract requires it. At the end of this phase, the pathway exists but nothing is in it.

items.s: Unit price and lump sum items, what each electrical item pays for, the quantity sheets, and the questions to ask before you price.
items.x: In one sentence: the Bid Item List says what you'll be paid for and how it's measured, so before pricing, know exactly what work each electrical item includes and which work is paid somewhere else or not at all. Unit price and lump sum Unit price items are paid by measured quantity (each, linear foot, cubic yard). Your price times the final measured quantity is what you get. Lump sum items are paid as one amount for everything described. On Caltrans projects, electrical systems are often paid as a lump sum per system, such as a lighting system, a signal and lighting system or a ramp metering system. Caltrans' design guidance says that when electrical work is paid by lump sum, all the work shown on an electrical plan view sheet is included in a single bid item. So the lump sum carries everything on that sheet: conduit, pull boxes, conductors, foundations, poles, equipment, testing, unless the specs pay it elsewhere. Where to look Bid Item List: item number, description, unit, quantity. Electrical plan sheets ("E", "ED" and "EQ" sheets) and quantity sheets: what's in each system. See project plans. Special provisions: the measurement and payment clause for each item. See special provisions. Standard Specifications: Sections 86 and 87 for electrical work. See standard specifications. Cost breakdown for lump sum items The Standard Specifications (Section 9 1.16, Progress Payments) provide for a cost breakdown of lump sum items, which the Resident Engineer uses to pay progress. Plan your lump sum so it can be broken down sensibly later; Caltrans asks the RE to correct unbalanced unit costs in the breakdown before approving it. Questions to ask before pricing 1. Which work is paid in which item, and which is included in others? 2. Is anything shown on the plans but paid in no item (so you carry it inside another)? 3. Are there state furnished materials? 4. Are there supplemental work items or force account? 5. What do the addenda change? Send questions through the Caltrans bidder inquiry process before the deadline; answers apply to all bidders. Official sources Caltrans Construction Manual, Section 86.

items.s: Building the submittal log from the contract, preparing submittals that get approved the first time, and tracking them.
items.x: In one sentence: a submittal is the product data, drawings or samples you send for approval before you order or install, and nothing should be installed without it. Building the log Go through the standard specifications and the special provisions and list every "submit": material lists, product data, shop and working drawings, test plans, certificates, schedules. On electrical jobs, Sections 86 and 87 and their Special Provisions produce most of the list. For each line: specification reference, description, submitted date, response, resubmittal, approval date. A submittal that gets approved Cover sheet with the contract number, the specification section and the item. Highlight the exact model, options and ratings on the cut sheet; cross out what doesn't apply. Show compliance: point to where each requirement is met. One subject per submittal , but complete. Include the Caltrans form or format the contract or the Resident Engineer requires. Review time The specifications set how long Caltrans has to review. Build that time, and a possible resubmittal, into the schedule. See procurement long lead. PM notes Submit long lead items first, and submit them complete: a returned submittal restarts the clock.

items.t: The day-to-day of a GC project manager
items.s: What a project manager at a small electrical general contractor actually does on Caltrans jobs, day by day and phase by phase.
items.x: In one sentence: the field crew builds the system; the project manager makes sure every piece is approved, ordered, delivered, installed, tested, documented and paid, in the right order. A typical day Morning: check the daily reports from the foremen, answer field questions, and look at what material the crew needs this week. See daily reports. Midday: chase submittals and RFIs with the Resident Engineer, call suppliers about lead times and deliveries. See submittals and rfis. Afternoon: update the schedule, prepare change order backup, plan the next lane closures, and file paperwork Caltrans needs to pay the job. What the PM owns Area What it means in practice Contract Knowing the Special Provisions, plans and bid items better than anyone on the job Submittals Getting every material and drawing approved before it is ordered or installed Procurement Quotes, purchase orders, lead times, deliveries. See procurement long lead Schedule The baseline CPM schedule and its updates RFIs and changes Asking the right questions in writing and getting paid for extra work. See change orders Documentation Daily reports, certificates, test results, as builts Closeout Getting the system accepted and the final package delivered. See closeout package Where the time goes by phase Early in a job, most time goes to reading the contract, submittals and long lead orders. In the middle, it is coordination: material arriving on time, the crew working in the right order, field problems turned into RFIs. At the end, it is testing, the punch list and paperwork. The lifecycle overview shows how the phases connect. The habit that matters most Write things down. A phone call that changes the work isn't a change until it is in writing. An RFI answered by email is evidence. A daily report that mentions a delay is the start of a claim. Caltrans pays for what is documented.

items.s: The two ways conduit goes underground on a highway job, when each one is used, and the risks of each.
items.x: In one sentence: trenching is open and predictable; boring avoids cutting pavement and traffic but hides what is underground. Trenching An open trench is cut, conduit is laid on bedding, and the trench is backfilled and the surface restored. Best for: shoulders, unpaved areas, short runs, many conduits together. Watch: traffic control, pavement restoration, compaction, and keeping the trench safe and short. Horizontal directional drilling (boring) A drill steers a pilot bore underground, then pulls the conduit back through it. Best for: crossing roadways, ramps, driveways, waterways or landscaped areas without opening them. Watch: utilities you can't see, the depth of the bore, frac outs (drilling fluid surfacing), and a bore log to record the actual path. Choosing The plans or specifications sometimes require one method for a location. Otherwise, choose on cost, traffic impact and risk. Boring is often done by a specialty subcontractor. PM notes Pothole the utilities the bore will cross before drilling. Keep the bore logs: they become the as built depth record. If a utility conflict forces a new route, write an RFI before changing it. See rfis.

items.s: How Caltrans detects vehicles: inductive loops, magnetometers, video and radar, and what each needs from the contractor.
items.x: In one sentence: detection tells signals, ramp meters and the TMC where vehicles are and how traffic is moving. Types Type How it works Notes Inductive loops Wire loops cut into the pavement; a vehicle changes their inductance Saw cutting and sealant; sensitive to pavement work Magnetometers Small in pavement sensors that sense the vehicle's magnetic field Often wireless to a nearby receiver Video detection Cameras with software that detects vehicles in zones Aiming and zone setup matter Radar Pole mounted sensors that measure presence or speed Used for counts and speeds on freeways The contract names the type and the layout on the plans. What the contractor installs Loops or sensors, lead in cable to the cabinet, detector cards or processors in the cabinet, and the setup (sensitivity, zones). See conductors and cables. Testing Loops are tested for inductance and insulation; every detector must report correctly to the controller or the TMC. See phase 9 system testing. PM notes Coordinate loops with paving: cut loops in new pavement only when the schedule allows, and protect existing loops during other work.

items.s: Taking off conduit, pull boxes, conductors, fiber, foundations, poles and equipment from Caltrans electrical sheets, and checking against the quantity sheets.
items.x: In one sentence: a good takeoff counts and measures every component on the electrical sheets by system and location, adds what the plans imply but don't show, and checks the totals against the quantity sheets. Set up before counting Organize the takeoff by bid item and system , then by location (station range, interchange, ramp). Use the same cost codes as your job costing. See job costing. Keep a list of every plan sheet and mark it when done. What to take off Component Measure Watch for Conduit Length by size, type and method (trench, bore, structure mounted) Method changes cost far more than length; riser and bend allowances. See conduit and trenching vs boring Pull boxes Count by type and size Traffic rated boxes, extensions, grounding. See pull boxes Conductors and cables Length by size and type, run by run Slack at boxes and poles, vertical runs, the number of conductors per run. See conductors and cables Fiber optic cable Length by count, splices, terminations Slack loops, splice closures, testing. See fiber optic communications Foundations Count by type Depth, rebar, anchor bolts, concrete. See foundations Poles and standards Count by type Mast arms, luminaire arms, lead time Equipment Count by type Cabinets, controllers, detection, cameras, signs Removals and modifications Count and describe Existing systems to keep running What the plans don't show Slack, waste and splices. Traffic control needed to reach each location. Testing and documentation. See electrical testing. Temporary systems to keep existing lighting or signals working. Checking the takeoff Compare your totals with the quantity sheets on the plans; explain every big difference. Have someone else check the largest items. Walk or drive the site if you can: access, existing conditions, conflicts. PM notes Save the takeoff with sheet references. When you win, it becomes the material order list and the foreman's quantity budget.

items.s: Roadway, interchange, sign and underpass lighting: poles, luminaires, circuits and controls.
items.x: In one sentence: highway lighting puts light where drivers need it at night: interchanges, ramps, signs and underpasses. Main parts Part What it does Lighting standards and arms Hold the luminaires. See foundations Luminaires LED fixtures; type and distribution set by the contract Sign lighting Lights overhead guide signs when required Soffit lighting Lights underpasses and structures Circuits and service Power from the service through the lighting circuits. See service equipment Controls Photocells or controllers that switch lights on at dusk How it is built Conduit and pull boxes, foundations, poles and arms, conductors, luminaires, then circuit tests and a night check. PM notes Lighting poles near traffic may need breakaway bases; follow the details. Check voltage drop on long circuits matches the design; conductor size comes from the plans. Do a night inspection before acceptance: every luminaire lit and aimed.
