Glossary: terms and abbreviations. Underlined terms in an article link there. Reading an article Each article starts with a one sentence summary, then explains what the thing is, how it is used on a job, and what a project manager should watch for. Most end with a Common mistakes box: what goes wrong in practice and what Caltrans checks. The sidebar shows the article's sections, linked articles and tags. What this wiki is not It is not Caltrans guidance and not a contract interpretation. Section numbers and requirements change between editions, and every contract's Special Provisions change the rules for that job. Always check the documents of your own contract, and ask the Resident Engineer in writing when something is unclear. Search Use the search box at the top of every page to find an article or a term.

items.s: Setting pull boxes and vaults on the conduit runs, and building cabinet, pole and sign foundations.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 3 creates the access points and the bases that everything above ground will stand on. Pull boxes Pull boxes and vaults are set where the conduit runs change direction, at devices, and at intervals along long runs, as shown on the plans. They include communication and fiber pull boxes. See pull boxes. Foundations Cast in place foundations for cabinets, signal and lighting poles, sign structures, camera poles and solar assemblies. Each one needs the right anchor bolts set to template, conduit stubs in the right place and a ground rod or grounding as detailed. See foundations. Inspection, then concrete Caltrans inspects the excavation, reinforcement, anchor bolts and conduit before the pour. Concrete must cure before a pole or cabinet is loaded on it. Keep the concrete delivery tickets; they are part of the closeout record. PM focus Anchor bolt templates and bolts ordered with the poles; they're often needed first. Inspection requested in time for the pour. Correct number and size of conduit stubs: missing one means breaking concrete later.

items.s: Getting quotes, issuing purchase orders and tracking long-lead equipment so it arrives when the crew needs it.
items.x: In one sentence: procurement turns approved submittals into material on site at the right time, and long lead items are where schedules slip. Typical long lead items on electrical jobs Controller and equipment cabinets. Poles, mast arms and anchor bolts. Changeable message signs and cameras. Batteries, especially lithium batteries with shipping rules. Network equipment: switches, routers, specific SFP modules. Fiber cable in specific fiber counts. The cycle 1. Quote: send suppliers the specification and plan references, not just a part number. 2. Submit the quoted product. See submittals. 3. Purchase order as soon as it is approved, or earlier with the supplier's agreement for very long lead times. 4. Track fabrication and shipping dates every week. 5. Receive: check the delivery against the PO and the approved submittal; note damage on the ticket. 6. Store safely, and keep certificates and manuals for closeout. Ordering bulk material For conduit, pull boxes, conductors and fittings, ask the foremen what is left before reordering, and keep a running takeoff against what is installed. See daily reports. PM notes Put procurement in the schedule with real lead times. A missing cabinet stops a system as surely as a missing crew.

items.t: Project plans: sheet types, legends and electrical sheets
items.s: How a set of Caltrans project plans is organized, how to find the electrical sheets, and how a PM reads them for takeoffs and field work.
items.x: In one sentence: the project plans show what to build on this job and where; the electrical sheets are the ones your crew will live in. How a plan set is organized A Caltrans plan set is a stack of sheets grouped by discipline. A typical order is: title sheet and location map, typical cross sections, layouts, construction details, stage construction and traffic handling, drainage, utilities, then the specialty sheets such as electrical , signs and striping, and structures. Each sheet has a title block with the sheet number, the total number of sheets, the contract number and the engineer's stamp. The electrical sheets Electrical sheets usually include: Electrical legend and abbreviations: the symbols for pull boxes, conduit, poles, cabinets and devices. Read it first; symbols differ between districts and designers. Plan sheets (layouts): where each pull box, conduit run, pole and cabinet goes, with stationing and offsets. Schedules and details: conductor and conduit schedules, pole and equipment schedules, wiring diagrams, cabinet details and system block diagrams. Communication sheets on ITS jobs: fiber routes, splice diagrams and network diagrams. The plans refer to standard details by Standard Plan number instead of drawing them. See standard plans es. How a PM uses them Takeoff: count devices and measure conduit and conductor runs to check the bid quantities. Note what is paid as a bid item and what is included in another item. Submittals and procurement: the schedules name the equipment to submit and order. See submittals. Field layout: stationing and offsets tell the crew where to stake. Written dimensions govern over scaling the drawing. See order of precedence. As builts: mark changes on a set of plans as the work happens; it becomes the as built record at closeout. See closeout package. When the plans disagree If the plans conflict with the special provisions, the Special Provisions govern. If the plans conflict with the field (a utility, a slope, a sign in the way), write an RFI. See rfis.

items.s: Underground access points along conduit runs: sizes, covers, extensions and grounding, and what to check before setting them.
items.x: In one sentence: a pull box is the buried box with a lid where crews pull, splice and later service the cables. What they are for Pull boxes break long conduit runs into lengths that can be pulled, give access at devices, poles and cabinets, and hold slack and splices. Larger vaults hold fiber splice closures and many conduits. Types and sizes Caltrans pull boxes come in standard numbered sizes, with covers and details shown on the ES Standard Plans. See standard plans es. The project plans show which size goes where. Communication and fiber pull boxes may be larger or specified in the special provisions. Item What it is for Concrete or polymer concrete box The body; polymer concrete is lighter and corrosion resistant Cover (lid) Secures the opening; marking shows the system (for example, electrical or communications) Extension Adds depth where needed Ground rod and bonding Grounds metal covers and equipment as detailed. See grounding and bonding Drain rock Lets water drain under the box Installation notes Set to grade, on drain rock, with conduit entering as detailed. Use traffic rated boxes and covers where vehicles can drive over them. Keep boxes clear of dirt; clean them before pulling cable and before acceptance. PM notes Pull boxes are often among the first materials needed. Order them with the conduit, and check the plan count against the bid item list.

items.s: What goes in a daily report on a Caltrans job and why it is the most important record you keep.
items.x: In one sentence: the daily report is the job's diary: it proves what was done, with whom, and what got in the way. .") What to record each day Date, contract and locations worked. Crew: names, classifications and hours. Equipment used. Work performed and quantities installed (feet of conduit, boxes set, foundations poured). Materials received. Subcontractors on site. Inspections and who from Caltrans was present. Delays and problems: weather, utility conflicts, waiting on answers, lane closure cancellations. Safety meeting held and topics. Photos. Why it matters Payment: quantities in daily reports support final quantities. Change orders and claims: a delay that isn't in the daily report is very hard to prove later. See change orders. Timesheets and certified payroll follow from the labor recorded. PM notes Make it easy for foremen to file the same day, from the field, with photos. Review them daily and follow up on anything that sounds like a change.

items.s: Cast-in-place foundations that support poles, cabinets and structures: anchor bolts, reinforcement, conduit stubs and inspection.
items.x: In one sentence: a foundation is the concrete base a pole or cabinet bolts onto, and it has to be right the first time. Types Pole foundations for signal and lighting standards, CCTV and communication poles: usually drilled, reinforced concrete piles. Cabinet foundations: a pad with conduit stubs coming up under the cabinet. Sign and solar foundations as detailed on the plans. Dimensions and reinforcement come from the standard plans es and the project plans. Materials Item What it is for Anchor bolts and templates Hold the pole or cabinet; the template sets the bolt pattern Rebar Reinforces the concrete Forms or sonotubes Shape the foundation above ground Concrete The foundation itself; keep the tickets Ground rod and conductor Grounding as detailed. See grounding and bonding Conduit stubs Bring the conduits up into the pole or cabinet Inspection The inspector checks the excavation, reinforcement, bolt pattern, conduit stubs and grounding before the pour. Concrete must cure before loading. See phase 3 pull boxes foundations. PM notes Anchor bolts often come with the poles but are needed weeks earlier. Order them first.

items.s: Installing poles, camera and communication poles, solar assemblies and equipment cabinets.
items.x: In one sentence: in phase 4 the job becomes visible: poles stand up and cabinets go on their foundations. What happens Poles: signal and lighting standards, mast arms, CCTV poles and communication poles, set on cured foundations and plumbed. Solar assemblies: panel mounts and battery enclosures at sites without utility power. See solar power and batteries. Equipment cabinets: set on foundations, sealed and grounded. See equipment cabinets. PM focus Deliveries in order: poles and cabinets are long lead items and need storage or same day setting. Lifting plans and lane closures for setting poles near traffic. Damage on arrival: inspect finishes and record any damage before signing the delivery ticket. Shop drawing match: height, arm length and bolt pattern match the approved submittal. After this phase, the structures exist, but they aren't wired.

items.t: Pricing labor: crews and production rates
items.s: Building crew costs at prevailing wage, choosing production rates from your own job history, and pricing night work, overtime and travel.
items.x: In one sentence: labor is the riskiest part of an electrical estimate, so price it as crews times days, using production rates from your own past jobs and the prevailing wage rates that apply to the project. The basic calculation 1. Quantity from the takeoff (for example, feet of 2 inch conduit in trench). 2. Production rate: how much one crew installs per day in these conditions. 3. Crew days = quantity / production rate. 4. Crew cost per day: each worker's hourly cost × hours, plus the crew's small tools and truck. 5. Labor cost = crew days × crew cost per day. Crew cost For each classification on the crew (for example inside wireman, laborer, operator, apprentice): the prevailing wage basic rate and fringe benefits for the county and craft, from the determination that applies on the bid advertisement date (see prevailing wage); payroll taxes and workers' compensation (your burden ); overtime and shift premiums where the work requires them. Production rates Use your own job cost history first: what the crew really achieved on similar work. See job costing. Adjust for conditions: night work, lane closure windows, hard digging, structure mounted conduit, traffic, travel to scattered locations. On freeway work, the closure window often controls production more than the work itself. Night work, overtime, travel Caltrans often limits work to specific hours and lane closures in the special provisions. Price the real working hours per shift, not eight. Overtime and shift premiums from the wage determination. Travel time and subsistence where the determination requires them. Supervision Foreman and general foreman time, and the PM's field time if it's charged to jobs, belong in labor or field overhead, not forgotten. PM notes Write the production rates and the crew you assumed into the estimate. When you win, the foreman gets the same numbers as the job's target.

items.s: The signals that release vehicles onto the freeway at a controlled rate: cabinet, signals, detection and communication.
items.x: In one sentence: a ramp meter is a small signal on an on ramp that lets cars onto the freeway one or two at a time, timed from what the detectors see. Main parts Part What it does Ramp meter controller and cabinet Runs the metering rate. See equipment cabinets Meter signal heads Red/green signals at the stop line Detection Demand, passage, queue and mainline detectors. See vehicle detection Signs Advance warning signs, sometimes with flashers Communication Link to the TMC for monitoring and rate changes. See network equipment How it works Detectors on the ramp and freeway tell the controller how much traffic there is. The controller sets the rate, and the TMC can monitor and change it remotely. PM notes Detector layout and lane numbering must match the plans exactly; the TMC reads them by number. Plan the turn on with Caltrans operations staff.

items.s: What the Caltrans Standard Plans are, what the ES electrical sheets cover, and how revised standard plans fit in.
items.x: In one sentence: the Standard Plans are Caltrans's book of standard drawings, and the ES sheets are the electrical details your project plans point to instead of drawing them again. What they are Caltrans publishes a set of Standard Plans alongside the standard specifications. Each sheet shows a standard detail used on many projects. The project plans reference a Standard Plan by its number, and that detail becomes part of the contract. Standard Plans are grouped by letter prefix by subject. The ES sheets cover electrical systems . What the ES sheets cover The ES series typically includes: Symbols and abbreviations used on electrical plans. Pull boxes: sizes, covers, installation and grounding. See pull boxes. Conduit installation details. See conduit. Foundations for signal, lighting and sign poles and for cabinets. See foundations. Poles, mast arms and luminaire arms for signals and lighting. Signal heads, mountings and detector loops. See traffic signals and vehicle detection. Service equipment and cabinet details. See service equipment and equipment cabinets. Sheet numbers and contents change between editions, so look up the exact sheet in the edition your contract names. Revised Standard Plans When a Standard Plan sheet changes after the edition was published, Caltrans issues a Revised Standard Plan (RSP) . RSPs that apply are included with the contract, and they govern over the original sheet. See order of precedence. How a PM uses them During takeoff: a single symbol on the plans may stand for a whole Standard Plan detail (the box, the cover, the grounding, the extension). Price the detail, not just the symbol. For submittals: standard details still need the materials submitted that meet them. In the field: give the crew the Standard Plan sheet with the project plan sheet. Many field questions are answered on the ES sheet. If the project plans show something different from the Standard Plan they reference, the project plans govern.

items.s: Traffic cameras that let the TMC watch the highway: cameras, poles, encoders and the network behind them.
items.x: In one sentence: CCTV cameras let the Traffic Management Center see incidents and conditions live and react. Main parts Part What it does Camera (PTZ or fixed) Pan tilt zoom cameras are remotely controlled; fixed cameras watch one view CCTV pole and mount Raises the camera for a clear view. See foundations Video encoder (if needed) Converts video to network streams for older or analog cameras Network equipment Switch, fiber or cellular router back to the TMC. See network equipment Surge protection On power and data at the pole. See surge protection Power Utility service or solar. See solar power and batteries Setup Cameras get IP addresses and settings from Caltrans, are added to the TMC's video system, and are aimed and given preset views. Testing Caltrans checks it can see the stream, control pan tilt zoom, and recall presets. See phase 9 system testing. PM notes Confirm camera model, video format and TMC software compatibility at submittal time. A camera the TMC can't read is a failed test.

items.s: How extra or changed work becomes a Contract Change Order, and how to document it so you get paid.
items.x: In one sentence: when the work changes, a Contract Change Order (CCO) changes the contract so you are paid for it. Where changes come from Differing conditions: potholing finds a utility where the conduit should go; the ground isn't what was expected. Caltrans changes: a device moves, equipment is added, a design changes. Document problems: an RFI answer that adds work. See rfis. How it works 1. Notify in writing promptly when you believe work is extra or changed. The specifications set notice requirements; missing them can cost the right to be paid. 2. Document: photos, daily reports, potholing results, RFI and answer. 3. Price: agreed lump sum, unit prices, or force account (tracked labor, equipment and materials). 4. CCO issued by Caltrans, signed by both sides, with any time extension. Force account When the price can't be agreed in advance, the work is paid on actual labor, equipment and materials plus markups. Daily force account records must be signed by the inspector each day. PM notes Keep a change log: description, date notified, status, value, time impact. Review it in every weekly meeting with the Resident Engineer.

items.s: Power conductors, grounding conductors, and signal, detector and communication cables: what each is for and how they are installed.
items.x: In one sentence: conductors carry power, and cables carry signals and data; both are pulled through the conduit and terminated in cabinets and devices. Power conductors Copper conductors sized and insulated as the specifications and conductor schedule require, from the service to the cabinets and devices. Color coding follows the specifications. Grounding conductors Bare or insulated conductors that bond equipment, poles and boxes to the grounding system. See grounding and bonding. Signal and communication cables Signal cable (multi conductor) from the controller cabinet to signal heads. See traffic signals. Detector lead in cable from loops or sensors to the cabinet. See vehicle detection. CAT6 and control cables for network devices. Fiber optic cable. See fiber optic communications. Installation notes Pull only after the conduit is proven clear. See phase 5 cable installation. Respect pulling tension and bend radius; use lubricant made for cable. Splice only where allowed, with the splice method specified. Label at both ends and in pull boxes. See labeling and identification. Test insulation before energizing. See electrical testing. PM notes Keep the reel tags and certifications for the submittal and closeout records.

items.s: Getting complete supplier quotes on time, checking them against the specs, and pricing long-lead equipment, escalation and sales tax.
items.x: In one sentence: send suppliers a clear list early, compare quotes line by line against the specs, and protect the bid against long lead times and price changes. Requesting quotes Send each supplier the list from your takeoff with spec references and sheet numbers, plus the special provisions sections that apply. Ask for unit prices, lead times, validity date, freight and exclusions. Ask early: a supplier who gets the list two days before the bid prices it in a hurry. Leveling quotes Put quotes side by side, item by item: Check Why Same items and quantities Missing items look cheap Spec compliance Approved products, Caltrans requirements, certifications. See submittals Lead time Must fit the schedule. See procurement long lead Validity and escalation How long the price holds Freight and delivery To the yard or the site Exclusions What the supplier didn't price Long lead and high value items Controllers, cabinets, poles, cameras, changeable message signs and some fiber equipment can take months. Check lead time against the working days and the contract's start, and note any risk. Escalation If quotes are valid only for a short time and the job won't order for months, add an allowance for price changes, or get the supplier to hold prices. Sales tax Price materials including sales tax at the rate where the work is done, unless the contract says otherwise. Federal aid jobs Federal aid contracts carry Buy America requirements for iron, steel and other products. Confirm with suppliers that their products comply. See federal aid davis bacon. PM notes Keep the leveled quote sheet. When you win, it's the purchasing plan, and suppliers will expect to hear from you first.

items.s: Pulling power conductors, fiber optic cable and communication cable through the finished conduit system.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 5 fills the pathway: conductors, fiber and communication cable are pulled from box to box. Before pulling Prove the conduit is continuous and clear. A blocked run found during a pull costs a lot more than one found with a mandrel. What is pulled Power: service conductors, branch circuits and grounding conductors. See conductors and cables. Fiber optic cable: backbone and distribution fiber, with slack loops left at pull boxes as specified. See fiber optic communications. Communication and control cable: CAT6, detector lead in, signal and control cables. Good practice Don't exceed the cable's pulling tension or bend radius, especially for fiber. Label each cable at both ends and in pull boxes as it is pulled. See labeling and identification. Keep the reel tags: they hold the cable data for submittals and records. At the end of this phase, everything is connected physically but nothing is terminated.

items.t: The bid package: bid items, quantities and the Bid Item List
items.s: What comes in a Caltrans bid package, how bid items and quantities work, and what a PM checks before pricing an electrical job.
items.x: In one sentence: the bid package is everything you need to price the job: the plans, the Special Provisions, the bid forms and the list of bid items you will be paid on. What is in it A Caltrans bid package usually contains: Notice to Bidders and Special Provisions: the bid date, working days, liquidated damages, the DBE goal, and the special provisions. Project plans. See project plans. Bid book: the bid forms and certifications, including the Bid Item List . Information handout or supplemental information when available: reports and reference material. Addenda issued before the bid date. Each one must be acknowledged. The standard specifications and standard plans es are part of the contract by reference; they aren't printed in the package. Bid items The Bid Item List is the list of things Caltrans pays for, each with an item number, a description, a unit (each, linear foot, lump sum) and an estimated quantity. You enter a unit price for each item. Two rules matter most: Payment follows the contract, not your cost. The payment clause in the specifications says what each item includes. Work that isn't a separate item is included in other items. Quantities are estimates for unit price items. You are paid for the quantity actually installed and measured; lump sum items are paid as a whole. On electrical jobs, systems are often paid as lump sum (for example, a signal and lighting system at one location), with some items such as conduit or fiber paid by the foot. What a PM checks before pricing 1. Read Sections 86 and 87 of the Special Provisions for equipment, testing and payment changes. 2. Do your own takeoff from the plans and compare it with the Bid Item List. 3. Mark long lead equipment and get supplier quotes early. See procurement long lead. 4. Check working days, lane closure restrictions and night work: they drive labor cost. 5. Note anything unclear and ask before the bid date through the bidders' inquiry process.

items.t: Caltrans acceptance testing and the punch list
items.s: Preparing for Caltrans witness tests, handling the punch list, and getting the system accepted.
items.x: In one sentence: acceptance is when Caltrans confirms the system works and is documented; the punch list is what stands between you and it. Before the witness test Your own tests are done and passed. See phase 9 system testing. Test reports are ready in the required format, with calibration certificates. The network is configured and devices report to the TMC. Cabinets are clean, labeled and have prints inside. During the test The Resident Engineer and inspectors, sometimes with district electrical or TMC staff, watch the tests and inspect the work. Have the crew, the fiber or network subcontractor, and test equipment on site. The punch list Common findings: labeling, missing documentation, grounding corrections, network configuration. Track every item to closure with photos. See phase 11 punch list. Acceptance Once the punch list is closed and the documents are delivered, Caltrans accepts the work (for a system or the whole contract) and maintenance responsibility passes to Caltrans. See closeout package.

items.s: Electronic signs that show messages sent from the TMC: the sign, its structure, controller and communication.
items.x: In one sentence: a changeable message sign (CMS) shows drivers messages the TMC sends: incidents, travel times, closures. Main parts Part What it does Sign housing and display LED display in a walk in or front access housing Sign structure Overhead or roadside structure and foundation, often by others Sign controller and cabinet Receives messages and runs the display. See equipment cabinets Communication Fiber or cellular link to the TMC. See network equipment Power Service with enough capacity for the display. See service equipment Testing Caltrans checks every pixel or module, brightness control, and that the TMC can post and clear messages. PM notes A CMS is a long lead item and heavy: plan delivery, lifting and lane closures together. Confirm the controller's protocol matches the TMC software at submittal time.

items.t: Equipment, traffic control and indirect costs
items.s: Pricing the equipment, traffic control, mobilization, field overhead, bonds and insurance that turn direct work into a complete bid.
items.x: In one sentence: the costs that aren't installed work (equipment, traffic control, mobilization, supervision, bonds and insurance) often decide whether a freeway electrical job makes money, so price them from the schedule, not as a percentage. Equipment List the equipment each crew needs (trencher, backhoe, bore rig, bucket truck, crane, compressor, generator) and how many days. Owned equipment at your internal rate; rented equipment at quote plus delivery. See buy rent or lease equipment. Price by days on the job, including idle days between closures. Traffic control On freeway electrical work, traffic control is often a major cost: check whether it's a separate bid item or included in others; count closures by type (shoulder, lane, ramp, full) and number of nights; get a quote from a traffic control sub, or price your own crew and equipment; include changeable message signs or flaggers where required. Mobilization and field overhead Mobilization: moving equipment and setting up; check the Bid Item List for a mobilization item and its limits. Field overhead: superintendent, project trucks, yard or storage, temporary facilities, testing, surveying, safety, cleanup. Price field overhead per working day or per month of the schedule. Schedule and working days The contract sets the working days. A schedule drives field overhead and equipment cost, so build at least a rough one: closures available per week, crews, sequence. Know the liquidated damages per day. Bonds, insurance, company overhead and profit Bid, performance and payment bonds: rate from your surety. See bid security and payment performance bonds. Insurance not already in labor burden. Company overhead recovery and profit. See overhead and markup. PM notes Indirect costs are where low bids lose money. Compare your total indirects with past jobs of similar length.

items.s: Connecting equipment, poles, boxes and cabinets to earth and to each other so faults clear and people stay safe.
items.x: In one sentence: grounding gives fault current and lightning a safe path to earth; bonding ties all the metal together so nothing becomes energized. What gets grounded and bonded Service equipment and cabinets, through ground rods and a ground bar. Metal poles, through their foundations. Metal pull box covers and conduit. Equipment inside cabinets, to the cabinet ground bar. Surge protection devices. See surge protection. Materials Item What it is for Ground rods Connect the system to earth Grounding and bonding conductors Tie metal parts together Ground bars Common point in a cabinet Clamps and connectors Approved connections, sometimes exothermic welds Testing Ground resistance is measured and must meet the value in the specifications. See electrical testing. PM notes Grounding is one of the most common acceptance findings. Have the crew photograph connections before they are buried or covered. See phase 10 acceptance testing.

items.s: Installing the electronics: power supplies, switches, routers, surge protection, batteries and field devices.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 6 puts the approved equipment in the cabinets and on the poles. Inside the cabinet Power supplies, surge protection, terminal blocks, Ethernet and fiber switches, routers, patch panels, and UPS or battery backup systems. See equipment cabinets, network equipment and surge protection. Power at remote sites Solar charge controllers, batteries and PV panels. See solar power and batteries. Field devices Cameras, detection equipment, network radios, sensors and signs. See cctv and video and vehicle detection. PM focus Install only what was approved in the submittal: model numbers must match. Record serial numbers as the equipment is installed; Caltrans will ask for them. Keep the manuals and warranty papers from every box; they go in the closeout package. See closeout package.

items.s: Everything Caltrans needs at the end of a job: as-builts, certifications, test results, warranties, manuals and final records.
items.x: In one sentence: the closeout package is the proof of what you built, and the job isn't finished until it is delivered and accepted. Checklist Document Notes As built plans Every change marked, with locations and depths Fiber splice diagrams Matching the field and the labels Test results Electrical, fiber and functional tests Material certifications Certificates of compliance for materials that need them Battery certifications Model, install date, warranty Concrete tickets For foundations and encasements Warranty documents With start dates Equipment manuals One set per device type, or as the contract requires Configuration files Final switch, router and device settings Serial number list By location Final CPM schedule Updated to actual dates Acceptance records Punch list closed, sign offs Final quantities Agree on the final measured quantity of every unit price item. Daily reports and measurements support them. See daily reports. PM notes Build the package from day one. File certificates with each submittal, tests as they are run, as builts as changes happen. See phase 12 closeout.

items.s: Fiber optic cable, splicing, termination and testing: the backbone that connects field devices to the TMC.
items.x: In one sentence: fiber carries data from cameras, signs, detectors and controllers back to the Traffic Management Center. Main parts Item What it is for Fiber optic cable Backbone and distribution cables, single mode, with the fiber count on the plans Innerduct Extra protection and organization inside conduit. See conduit Splice closures Protect splices in vaults and pull boxes Splice trays Hold and organize individual splices Patch panels Terminate fibers in cabinets Fiber jumpers Connect patch panels to equipment Labels Identify every fiber and port. See labeling and identification Installation Pull with tension control, leave slack loops where specified, splice by fusion, terminate in patch panels, and follow the splice diagram on the plans. See phase 7 fiber splicing. Testing OTDR: shows each event (splice, connector, break) along the fiber and its loss. Insertion loss with a power meter and light source: the total loss of each link. The contract sets wavelengths, directions and pass limits. Clean and inspect every connector before testing. PM notes Fiber work is often subcontracted. Agree on the splice plan, the test report format and the as built splice diagram before work starts.

items.s: Fusion splicing, splice closures and trays, termination at patch panels, and documenting losses.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 7 turns pulled fiber into working links, and the test records from it are what prove the links work. What happens Fusion splicing fiber to fiber in splice closures in vaults or pull boxes, and at the cabinets. Splice trays organize the splices; every fiber goes to a known position. Termination at patch panels in the cabinets, with connectors on the field side and jumpers to the equipment. Splice records: which fiber goes where, following the splice diagram on the plans. Testing OTDR traces show each splice and connector along the fiber and its loss. Power meter (insertion loss) tests measure the total loss end to end. The contract sets which tests, at which wavelengths, in which directions, and the loss limits. See fiber optic communications. The question this phase answers: is there continuity from the field device back to the TMC? PM focus Fiber splicing is often a specialty subcontractor. Agree early on the test format Caltrans wants and on who produces the as built splice diagram.

items.s: How power gets from the utility to the job: the service point, meter, disconnects and breakers, and the utility coordination it takes.
items.x: In one sentence: the service is where the utility's power becomes Caltrans's power, and getting it energized is often on the critical path. What it includes Item What it is for Service enclosure or pedestal Houses the meter, main disconnect and breakers Meter (when required) Measures energy for the utility bill Main disconnect and breakers Isolate and protect circuits Service conductors From the utility point of connection to the enclosure Grounding Ground rods and bonding at the service. See grounding and bonding Details are on the standard plans es and the project plans. Utility coordination The utility (for example, the local power company) decides the point of connection and schedules the connection. That usually takes an application, a service request from the agency, and inspection. Lead times can be long. PM notes Start the service request in phase 1; ask the Resident Engineer who files it on this contract. Plan temporary power or a generator if equipment must run before the service is energized. Sites with no practical utility service use solar. See solar power and batteries.

items.s: Getting and comparing sub quotes, DBE and listing requirements, and a bid day routine that gets a correct bid in on time.
items.x: In one sentence: bid day is about getting late numbers into a bid that's already built, so organize the sub quotes, the forms and the decisions before the morning, and leave time to check. Subcontractor quotes Common subs on electrical jobs: traffic control, boring, paving and concrete repair, striping, saw cutting, surveying, trucking. Send each sub the scope, plan sheets and spec sections early. Ask for exclusions, insurance, DIR registration and license. Level quotes by scope: the lowest number often excludes something. DBE and subcontractor listing If the contract has a DBE goal , plan how you'll meet it or document good faith efforts. See dbe requirements. California's subcontractor listing law requires listing subs above the threshold with their work and location; once listed, replacing them is restricted. See subcontractor listing. Before bid day All direct costs priced, with plugs for numbers still to come. Bid forms, bid bond, certifications and DBE forms prepared. See preparing a public bid and bid security. Electronic bidding set up and tested. Decide who has the final word on price, and the markup range. Bid day 1. Morning: last sub and supplier quotes arrive; replace plugs. 2. Level late quotes quickly; confirm scope on the phone if needed. 3. Final review of totals, markups and big items. See checking your bid. 4. Finish listing and DBE information. 5. Submit electronically with margin before the deadline. Caltrans allows resubmitting before the opening if you need to correct. PM notes Set a cut off time for quotes well before the deadline. A bid submitted in the last minutes is a bid nobody checked.

items.t: Checking your bid before it goes
items.s: Arithmetic and scope checks, comparison with historical Caltrans prices, unbalanced bids, and the questions to ask before you commit.
items.x: In one sentence: a quick but disciplined review catches the mistakes that lose money (missing scope, wrong units, arithmetic) and tells you whether your price makes sense against history. Scope check Every bid item priced, every plan sheet taken off, every addendum included. Work paid in no item carried somewhere. Sub and supplier exclusions covered. Arithmetic and units Unit prices times quantities equal item totals; the total adds up. Units match the Bid Item List (each, LF, LS). Large items reviewed by a second person. Comparing with history Caltrans' Contract Cost Data database lets you search historic bid prices by item, year and district. Use it to compare your unit prices for similar items; Caltrans advises limiting searches to your district and nearby districts and ignoring outliers. Your own past bids and job costs are the better comparison for your crews. Balanced bids On unit price items, keep each price close to its real cost plus a fair share of overhead and profit. Heavily unbalanced bids (very high prices on some items, very low on others) can be rejected, and they backfire when quantities change. On lump sum systems, the later cost breakdown should also be reasonable. Risk questions before committing Which three items carry the most risk, and is that risk priced? Can you staff it when it runs? Is the margin enough for the risk? See when to pass on a job. PM notes Keep a one page bid summary: totals by cost type, labor hours, crew days, key assumptions, plugs used, and who approved the final price. Official sources Caltrans Contract Cost Data.

items.s: The field cabinets that house controllers, network equipment and power: types, accessories, and what Caltrans checks.
items.x: In one sentence: the cabinet is the field office of every system: it holds the electronics, protects them from weather and intruders, and is where Caltrans technicians will work. What goes inside Controllers (signals, ramp meters), power supplies, surge protection, terminal blocks, switches, routers, patch panels and battery backup, depending on the system. See traffic signals, ramp metering and network equipment. Types Caltrans uses standard cabinet models for signals and ramp meters, and specified cabinets for communication hubs and ITS sites. The model is named in the plans or special provisions. Cabinets are often furnished pre wired by a manufacturer and may need factory testing before delivery. Accessory What it is for Cabinet base or riser Interface with the foundation Door switch Alarms when the cabinet is opened Fans, vents and thermostat Keep electronics cool Heater Prevents condensation Lighting and convenience outlet For technicians Surge protection Protects the electronics. See surge protection PM notes Cabinets are long lead items. Submit early. See procurement long lead. Check the approved wiring diagram against the cabinet on delivery. Keep the cabinet wiring prints inside the cabinet at turnover.

items.t: Network equipment: switches, routers, SFPs and cellular
items.s: The equipment that puts field devices on the Caltrans network: switches, routers, SFP modules, antennas and patch cords.
items.x: In one sentence: network equipment lets every device in the field talk to the TMC, over fiber or cellular. Main parts Item What it is for Ethernet switches Connect devices in the cabinet; managed, industrial rated Fiber switches Connect the cabinet to the fiber network SFP modules Plug in transceivers that connect a switch port to fiber Cellular routers Wireless link to the network where there is no fiber Antennas Cellular signal for the router Patch cords and CAT6 Connect equipment in the cabinet and to nearby devices The models are usually named or specified in the special provisions; the plans include a network diagram. Configuration IP addresses, VLANs, management access and security settings from Caltrans's network plan. See phase 8 network configuration. PM notes Match SFPs to the fiber type, wavelength and distance; the wrong SFP is a common cause of a dead link. Cellular routers need carrier service set up; confirm who provides the SIM and data plan. Save every final configuration file for the closeout package. See closeout package.

items.s: Programming switches and routers, assigning IP addresses and VLANs, and proving remote access.
items.x: In one sentence: in phase 8 the hardware is programmed so that each device can talk to Caltrans. What is configured Switches (managed industrial Ethernet or fiber switches): ports, VLANs, management addresses. Cellular routers at sites without fiber: carrier, VPN or tunnel settings Caltrans specifies. IP addresses for every device, from the plan Caltrans provides. Device settings: cameras, detectors, signs and controllers set up to report to the TMC. What is verified Communication paths from each device to the TMC. Remote access works the way Caltrans requires. Security settings: default passwords changed, unused ports disabled, firmware as approved. PM focus Get the IP plan and network requirements from Caltrans early: they are often the last piece to arrive. Many projects are physically finished but stay open until networking works. See network equipment.

items.t: After the bid: results, award and lessons
items.s: Reading the bid summary, what happens if you are low, and turning every result into better estimates.
items.x: In one sentence: every bid result, won or lost, tells you something about your prices, so read the bid summary, act quickly if you're low, and feed the lessons into the next estimate. Bid results Caltrans opens bids publicly and publishes results on its Bid Summary pages, with every bidder's total and, once verified, item prices. Bid openings for electronic bids can be watched online. If you're the apparent low bidder Watch for post bid requirements and deadlines in the special provisions and bid forms: DBE information, good faith effort documentation, other forms. See dbe requirements. Confirm your subs and suppliers right away. The low bidder is not the contractor until the award; protests and responsiveness reviews come first. See bid opening award protests. After award: contract execution, bonds, insurance. See payment performance bonds. If you're not Compare item by item with the low bidder and the second bidder: Where were you much higher or lower? Was it labor, material, a sub, or indirect costs? Did someone see a different method or a different reading of scope? Building your history Keep a simple log of every bid: project, district, scope, your total, the low total, the spread, your rank, and notes. Over time it shows where you're competitive and which agencies and job types to pursue. See choosing your market and finding public bids. From estimate to budget When you win, the estimate becomes the job budget: quantities, crew days and production rates by cost code. Hand it to the PM and foreman at the job start meeting. See project management small company. Official sources Caltrans Office Engineer: Bidder's Guide.

items.s: The contractor's own electrical, communication and functional tests before Caltrans witnesses anything.
items.x: In one sentence: phase 9 is your own test run: find and fix the problems before Caltrans comes to watch. Electrical tests Voltage, insulation resistance, continuity, grounding, battery operation and solar charging. See electrical testing. Communication tests Fiber performance, router and switch communication, and each device reachable on the network. Functional tests Test the system the way Caltrans will use it: Can Caltrans see the camera? Can it reach the switch and the field cabinet? Do the alarms (door open, power fail) reach the TMC? Does the signal, sign or meter do what the plans say? PM focus Write every result down in the format of the final test report. A test you can't show didn't happen. Schedule the Caltrans witness tests only after your own tests pass. See acceptance testing punch list.

items.s: Powering remote sites without utility power: panels, charge controllers, batteries and sizing.
items.x: In one sentence: where there is no practical utility service, solar panels charge batteries that run the site day and night. Main parts Item What it is for Solar panels Generate electricity Panel mounts Support and tilt the panels on the pole or structure Charge controller Regulates battery charging and protects the batteries Batteries (often LiFePO4) Store energy for night and cloudy days Battery enclosure and trays Hold and protect the batteries Battery cables and DC disconnect Connect the bank; let crews isolate it safely Sizing The design sets panel and battery capacity from the load (camera, radio, router) and the days of autonomy required. Don't substitute smaller equipment. Batteries Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries are common for their life and safety, and some contracts require them. They are long lead items with shipping rules for lithium batteries. See procurement long lead. Testing Caltrans may check charging, battery voltage, and that the site runs on battery alone. See phase 9 system testing.

items.s: Devices that protect field electronics from lightning and power surges, and where they go.
items.x: In one sentence: surge protection diverts voltage spikes to ground before they reach the electronics. Where it goes On the power service and the cabinet's main power input. On signal and data lines that leave the cabinet: detector lead ins, Ethernet to pole mounted devices, antenna feeds. On equipment as the specifications or the manufacturer require. How it works A surge protective device connects between the line and ground. It only works if the grounding is good, so it depends on grounding and bonding. PM notes Submit the devices specified for each location; they differ by voltage and signal type. Many devices have a status indicator. Check that they are healthy before acceptance.

items.s: Systems that keep traffic signals and field equipment running during power outages.
items.x: In one sentence: a battery backup system (BBS) keeps a signal or cabinet running for a time when utility power fails. Main parts Item What it is for Inverter and charger Switches to battery power and recharges afterward Batteries Stored energy, sized for the required run time Transfer switch / bypass Lets maintenance bypass the system Enclosure or cabinet space Houses the system, sometimes beside the controller cabinet Alarms Report power failure and battery status How it works When utility power drops, the system transfers to battery. Depending on the specification, a signal may run normally for a time, then switch to flashing operation to stretch the battery. Testing Pull the utility power and confirm the transfer, run time and alarms. PM notes Check battery shipping and storage rules, and record the battery install date; batteries have a service life and warranty that start then.

items.s: Caltrans witnesses the tests, reviews the documents and produces the punch list.
items.x: In one sentence: in phase 10 Caltrans checks that what you built works and is documented, before it takes the system over. What you provide Test reports, fiber test results, material certifications, as builts and warranty information. What Caltrans does The Resident Engineer and electrical inspectors witness the tests, sometimes with the district's electrical maintenance or TMC staff, and produce a list of deficiencies: the punch list. Common findings Labeling issues. Missing documentation. Grounding corrections. Network configuration corrections. PM focus Book the witness tests with enough notice, have the crew and any subcontractors on site, and bring the test reports printed. See acceptance testing punch list.

items.t: Pull tape, tracer wire and warning tape
items.s: The small items that make conduit usable and findable later: pull tape, tracer wire and buried warning tape.
items.x: In one sentence: these cheap items decide whether the next crew can use and find your conduit years from now. Item What it is for Pull tape (mule tape) Left inside conduit to pull cable later; often marked in feet Tracer wire Lets locators find non metallic conduit and fiber from the surface Warning tape Buried above the conduit to warn the next excavator Notes Leave pull tape in every empty or spare conduit, tied off at both ends. Make tracer wire continuous, with access points in pull boxes, and test it. Place warning tape at the depth the specifications or plans show. These are rarely paid as separate items, so they are easy to forget. They are also easy for an inspector to check.

items.s: The tests that prove an electrical installation is safe and complete: continuity, insulation resistance, ground resistance and functional tests.
items.x: In one sentence: testing proves the wiring is right before it is energized, and the test records prove it to Caltrans. Common tests Test What it proves Continuity Each conductor runs where it should, without breaks Insulation resistance Insulation is not damaged; no path to ground Ground resistance The grounding system meets the required value. See grounding and bonding Voltage and polarity Correct supply at each panel and device Functional test The system does what it is meant to do The tests required, how they are done and the pass values are in the specifications and special provisions. Test equipment Multimeters, insulation testers and ground resistance testers. Keep calibration certificates; Caltrans may ask for them. Fiber has its own tests. See fiber optic communications. PM notes Record results in the format of the final test report as you go. See phase 9 system testing and acceptance testing punch list.

items.s: Fixing every deficiency Caltrans found, and proving each one is fixed.
items.x: In one sentence: the punch list is the last quality check before turnover: close every item and get each one signed off. Typical items Missing or wrong labels. Damaged equipment or finishes. Documentation updates. Final adjustments: aiming cameras, timing, settings. How to run it 1. Turn the list into a tracker: item, location, who fixes it, date fixed, date Caltrans accepted. 2. Group items by location so the crew can fix them in one trip and one lane closure. 3. Photograph each fix. 4. Send the updated list to the Resident Engineer and ask for sign off. The job isn't accepted until the punch list is closed. See acceptance testing punch list.

items.s: Labels on conductors, cables, fibers, pull boxes and equipment, and why they are one of the most common punch-list items.
items.x: In one sentence: labels let Caltrans maintenance find and fix things for the next twenty years. What gets labeled Conductors and cables at both ends and in every pull box. Fibers, splice trays and patch panel ports , matching the splice diagram. Pull box covers with the system marking. Cabinets, breakers and equipment , matching the as builts. Good practice Use the label format and material the specifications call for: durable, readable, weather proof. Label as you pull and terminate, not at the end. Keep labels consistent with the plans, the splice diagram and the as builts. Why it matters Labeling is one of the most frequent findings in phase 10 acceptance testing. Fixing labels after the fact means reopening boxes and cabinets, often with a lane closure.

items.s: Delivering as-builts, certificates, test results and warranties, reconciling final quantities, and turning the system over.
items.x: In one sentence: closeout turns a finished system into an accepted contract and the final payment. Documentation As built plans, material certifications, fiber splice diagrams, test results, warranty packages, equipment manuals and configuration files. See closeout package. Administrative Final quantity reconciliation: agree with Caltrans on the measured quantity of every unit price item. Final schedule update. Final reports and any remaining certified payroll or compliance documents. Change orders all executed. See change orders. Turnover The system is transferred to Caltrans operations and maintenance. After acceptance, the warranty period starts. PM focus Start building the closeout package on day one: certificates with submittals, test results as they are run, as builts as changes happen. Closeout is slow when it starts at the end.

items.t: What makes a job public works in California
items.s: The definition that triggers prevailing wage, registration, payroll reporting and bonds, and the thresholds that matter.
items.x: In one sentence: a job is public works when it is construction, alteration, demolition, installation or repair done under contract and paid for in whole or in part with public money, and that one fact brings a whole set of rules with it. The definition California's prevailing wage law starts at Labor Code section 1720. The core test is simple: construction work, under contract, paid in whole or in part out of public funds . "Construction" is read broadly. It includes installation and repair, and it reaches work done before and after the main construction, such as surveying, inspection and hauling of materials to and from the site in many cases. Maintenance work is covered too. Public funds are also read broadly. A city paying the invoice is the obvious case. But fee waivers, below market land, low interest loans and other subsidies to a private developer can make a privately owned project public works as well. Who the owner is State agencies , such as Caltrans, which awards and manages its own highway contracts. See what a caltrans electrical contractor does. Local agencies : cities, counties, school districts, water and transit districts, community colleges. Private owners whose project receives public money of the kind described above. Each owner adds its own front end documents to the contract, but the state laws below apply to all of them. What comes with it Rule What it means for you Read more DIR registration You can't bid or work without a current registration dir registration Prevailing wage Workers are paid at least the published rate for their craft and county prevailing wage Certified payroll Weekly payroll records, reported electronically to DIR certified payroll Apprentices Notify apprenticeship programs and employ apprentices in ratio apprentices on public works Subcontractor listing List subs above the threshold in your bid subcontractor listing Bonds Bid security, then payment and performance bonds payment performance bonds No mechanics liens Unpaid parties use stop payment notices and bond claims instead stop payment notices The thresholds worth remembering $25,000 / $15,000: DIR registration and most state enforcement apply to construction projects over $25,000 and maintenance projects over $15,000. Below those amounts you may still owe prevailing wage. $1,000: prevailing wage itself applies to public works over $1,000, so small jobs are not exempt from paying the rate. $30,000: apprenticeship obligations apply to contracts of $30,000 or more. $25,000: a payment bond is required on public works contracts over $25,000. These numbers come from state law and can change; the bid documents for each job restate the ones that apply. Federal money When a job is paid partly with federal transportation funds (a "federal aid" job), federal rules are added on top: Davis Bacon wages, the FHWA 1273 required provisions and, at times, DBE requirements. See federal aid davis bacon.

items.t: Getting ready for your first public works job
items.s: The checklist to finish before you bid: license, DIR registration, bonding, insurance, payroll and apprenticeship.
items.x: In one sentence: most of what makes public works hard is set up once, before the first bid, and then kept current. Before you bid 1. The right contractor license. The license class must match the work, and it must be active when you submit the bid. See contractor license classes. 2. DIR public works contractor registration. No registration, no bid. Renew it every fiscal year or buy several years at once. See dir registration. 3. A surety relationship. You will need a bid bond with almost every bid and payment and performance bonds after award. A surety needs your financial statements, work history and personal indemnity, so start early. See surety bonding. 4. Insurance that matches public contracts. General liability, auto, workers' compensation and often an umbrella, with the endorsements agencies ask for. See insurance for public works. 5. A way to find bids. Agency portals, plan rooms, builders' exchanges. See finding public bids. Before your crew starts 1. Payroll that can produce certified payroll. Each worker's classification, hours by day, rate, fringe benefits and deductions, every week. See certified payroll. 2. Prevailing wage rates for the job. Download the determinations for each craft and county in effect on the bid advertisement date. See prevailing wage. 3. Apprenticeship paperwork. Send the DAS 140 within 10 days of signing and request apprentices with the DAS 142 when you need them. See apprentices on public works. 4. Subcontractor checks. License and DIR registration for every sub and lower tier sub, before they set foot on site. 5. Federal aid extras, if the job has federal money. See federal aid davis bacon. Keep current DIR registration renews by July 1 for the next fiscal year. License, insurance certificates and bond capacity: track expiration dates. Prevailing wage determinations change, usually in February and August; the rates for a job are fixed at bid advertisement, with scheduled increases built into many determinations. PM notes Write down who in the office owns each item. On a small company, payroll compliance often falls between the PM and the bookkeeper, and that is where penalties come from.

items.t: Who is who on a public works job
items.s: The awarding body, its engineer, the prime, subcontractors, suppliers, the surety and the state enforcement offices.
items.x: In one sentence: on public works, more people have a say in your job than on private work, and each one has a specific role you can lean on or must answer to. The parties under contract Awarding body (the agency): Caltrans, a city, a county, a district. It advertises, awards, pays and accepts the work. Its governing body (city council, board) often has to approve the award and change orders above a limit. The agency's engineer: on Caltrans jobs the Resident Engineer; on local jobs a city engineer, construction manager or consultant acting for the agency. Answers RFIs, approves submittals and changes, measures quantities for payment. Prime contractor (direct contractor): signs the contract with the agency and is responsible for all the work, including what its subs do. Subcontractors: perform part of the work for the prime, or for another sub (lower tier). Listed in the bid when above the threshold. See subcontractor listing. Suppliers: sell materials. They have payment rights too. See stop payment notices. Surety: the bonding company that guarantees the prime's bid, performance and payment. See surety bonding. The parties overseeing the job Department of Industrial Relations (DIR): registers contractors, publishes prevailing wage rates and receives certified payroll. See dir registration. Labor Commissioner's Office: enforces prevailing wage and apprenticeship; can audit and issue penalty assessments. See labor compliance penalties. Division of Apprenticeship Standards (DAS): apprenticeship programs and ratios. See apprentices on public works. Contractors State License Board (CSLB): licenses. Federal agencies on federal aid jobs, through the state: FHWA rules carried in the contract. PM notes Know the names behind each role on your job in the first week: the engineer, the agency's labor compliance contact and your surety's agent. Problems get solved faster when you know who to call.

items.s: Which CSLB license classes fit which work, and why the license must be active when you submit the bid.
items.x: In one sentence: the Contractors State License Board license is the first gate: the class must fit the work you bid, and on public works it must be active when you submit the bid, not just when you start. The classes you will see most on public works Class Name Typical public work A General Engineering Highways, bridges, utilities, earthwork, pipelines, and the civil side of electrical work B General Building Buildings, where the contract involves at least two unrelated trades C 10 Electrical Lighting, signals, service equipment, wiring C 7 Low Voltage Systems Communications and low voltage systems C 12 Earthwork and Paving Grading, paving C 32 Parking and Highway Improvement Striping, signs, barriers C 61/D xx Limited specialty Narrow scopes such as fencing or sign installation Bid documents state which classes are acceptable, sometimes as "Class A or C 10 at the time of bid". Read that line before anything else. When the license must be active California's Business and Professions Code requires that a contractor bidding public works be licensed in the right class when the bid is submitted . An unlicensed bid is nonresponsive and can bring penalties. Federal aid jobs follow a slightly different timing rule set by federal law, but the bid documents will say so. Your subcontractors Every sub needs a license in the class for its own scope, and its license number goes on your subcontractor list. A missing or wrong number can be corrected within 24 hours of bid opening if it was an inadvertent error, but a sub with no license is a real problem. See subcontractor listing. The qualifier A license is held through a qualifying individual (the RME or RMO) who passed the exam. If that person leaves, the license has a short window to replace them. Keep this in mind for a company that depends on one person. PM notes Check every license on the CSLB website the day you list a sub, and save a screenshot in the bid file.

items.t: California C-10 Electrical Contractor Exam: Full Study Guide
items.s: How the CSLB C-10 trade exam works, the code articles, tables and math to know cold, each of the five exam sections, practice problems and an eight-week study plan.
items.x: An independent study guide for the CSLB Electrical (C 10) trade examination, built around the official CSLB content outline and written for people who work in public works and infrastructure. Read this first. This guide is a study aid, not an official CSLB document. Code section numbers refer to the NEC structure used by the 2025 California Electrical Code (which is based on the 2023 NEC). Always confirm numbers, tables and values in your own code book. The exam is closed book, so the goal is to know this material, not to look it up. Fees, rules and exam content change; check cslb.ca.gov before you apply. 1. How the exam works Item What the CSLB says Format Multiple choice, four choices, one BEST answer Math Some calculation questions; a calculator is provided References Closed book; no materials allowed in the exam Guessing No penalty, so answer every question Time Plenty of time is given; read every choice before answering Authors Questions are written and reviewed by working licensed contractors The guide shows three question styles. Prepare for all three: 1. Code and requirement questions. Example topic: bonding and grounding of modules and metal mounting equipment on a roof PV system. 2. Selection questions. Example topic: what to check when replacing a branch circuit breaker (frame type, AIC rating, ampacity). 3. Calculation questions. Example topic: total cost with unit price, sales tax and a buy ten get one free promotion. Exam weights (approximate) Section Weight Priority 1. Planning and Estimating 28% Highest 2. Rough Wiring 27% Highest 5. Safety 18% High 4. Startup, Troubleshooting and Maintenance 16% Medium 3. Finish Wiring and Trim 11% Lower Planning/Estimating plus Rough Wiring is about 55% of the exam. Energy production and storage (photovoltaic, wind, generators, batteries, capacitors) appears inside four of the five sections , so do not skip it. 2. Official reference books The questions are drawn from these sources. You do not need to memorize every page, but you should be fluent in the first two. 2025 California Electrical Code (Title 24, Part 3) Cal/OSHA Title 8: General Industry & Electrical Safety Orders and Construction & Electrical Safety Orders (2025) 2025 California Building Code, Energy Code and Fire Code (Title 24) American Electricians' Handbook (McGraw Hill Professional) Photovoltaic Systems (American Technical Publishers) Ugly's Electrical References (Jones & Bartlett Learning) California code books can be viewed free online through the Building Standards Commission (dgs.ca.gov/bsc). Cal/OSHA Title 8 is viewable at dir.ca.gov. 3. Math you must be able to do fast Core formulas Ohm's law: E = I × R Power: P = E × I (watts); single phase VA = V × A Three phase VA = 1.732 × V × A Three phase current: I = VA ÷ (1.732 × V) Voltage drop, single phase: VD = (2 × K × I × L) ÷ CM (K = 12.9 for copper, 21.2 for aluminum; L is one way length in feet; CM is circular mils) Three phase voltage drop: replace the 2 with 1.732 Suggested limits (informational): 3% on a branch circuit or feeder, 5% total to the farthest outlet Percentage: % drop = VD ÷ source voltage × 100 Worked examples Continuous load, conductor and breaker. A 10 kW, 240 V single phase heater that runs continuously: I = 10,000 ÷ 240 = 41.7 A Continuous load at 125% = 52.1 A Breaker: next standard size = 60 A Conductor: 8 Cu at 75°C carries 50 A (too small); 6 Cu at 75°C carries 65 A (good) Voltage drop. 240 V, 40 A load, 150 ft one way, 8 Cu (16,510 CM): VD = (2 × 12.9 × 40 × 150) ÷ 16,510 = 9.38 V , or 3.9% (too high) Try 6 Cu (26,240 CM): VD = 5.90 V, or 2.5% (acceptable) Three phase current. A 30 kVA load on 208 V three phase: I = 30,000 ÷ (1.732 × 208) = 83.3 A Box fill. A box holds three 12/2 NM cables with ground and one switch: Six insulated conductors = 6 One device (yoke) = 2 All grounds together = 1 Total = 9 allowances × 2.25 in³ ( 12) = 20.25 in³ minimum box volume Estimating. 25 pieces at $4.20 each, 7.25% sales tax: 25 × $4.20 = $105

items.t: California Class A General Engineering Exam: Full Study Guide
items.s: How the CSLB Class A trade exam works, the math and numbers to know cold, each of the eight exam sections, practice problems and an eight-week study plan.
items.x: An independent study guide for the CSLB General Engineering (A) trade examination, built around the official CSLB content outline and written for people who work in public works and infrastructure. Read this first. This guide is a study aid, not an official CSLB document. Numbers, slopes, depths and test values are the commonly used ones; project specifications, Caltrans documents and the current Cal/OSHA orders govern in practice, so confirm every value in the reference books. The exam is closed book, so the goal is to know this material, not to look it up. Fees, rules and exam content change; check cslb.ca.gov before you apply. 1. What a Class A license is The General Engineering (A) classification covers fixed works that need specialized engineering knowledge and skill: roads and highways, bridges, tunnels, underground utilities and pipelines, sewer and water systems, drainage, flood control, grading, dams and similar infrastructure. It is the classic prime contractor license for public works such as Caltrans and city or county projects. Things to know: A Class A contractor can bid and manage jobs that combine several trades, but specialty work (for example electrical) must be performed under the right specialty license, either the contractor's own or a subcontractor's. The exam tests the whole job: planning, earthwork, piping, concrete, safety and traffic control, not one trade deeply. 2. How the exam works Item What the CSLB says Format Multiple choice, four choices, one BEST answer Math Some calculation questions; a calculator is provided References Closed book; no materials allowed Guessing No penalty, so answer every question Time Generous; read every question and all four choices Exam weights (approximate) Section Weight Priority 4. Subsurface, Surface and Elevated Piping Work 21% Highest 8. Safety 18% Highest 1. Planning and Estimating 15% High 3. Earthwork and Surveying 15% High 5. Foundation and Concrete Construction 11% Medium 6. Buildings, Structures and Related Work 9% Medium 2. Structural Principles 6% Lower 7. Roadwork and Paving 5% Lower Piping, Safety, Planning/Estimating and Earthwork together are about 70% of the exam. Spend your time there first. Question styles in the official guide The guide's sample questions show the flavor. One asks which connection is used to flush a water line (a blow off valve). One asks why the rate of pour is supervised for high wall forms (to avoid form collapse). One asks for the approximate backfill after removing a 10,000 gallon underground tank (about 50 cubic yards). So expect practical "what would you do or use" questions plus volume math. 3. Official reference books 2025 California Building Code, Electrical Code and Plumbing Code (Title 24) ACI 318, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete California Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA MUTCD), Part 6, temporary traffic control Excavation and Grading Handbook (Craftsman Book Company) Fundamentals of Building Construction: Materials and Methods (Allen and Iano, Wiley) Moving the Earth: Excavation Equipment, Methods, Safety, and Cost (McGraw Hill) Caltrans Standard Plans and Standard Specifications Cal/OSHA Title 8 General Industry and Electrical Safety Orders and Construction Safety Orders (2025) California code books can be viewed free online through the Building Standards Commission, and Cal/OSHA Title 8 is viewable at dir.ca.gov. 4.
