items.s: Why structures are inspected, what an inspector looks for, and where non-destructive testing fits.
items.x: In one sentence: inspection answers three questions about a structure: what condition is it in, why, and what should be done about it, and non destructive testing (NDT) is how you look beyond the surface without damaging it. Why structures are inspected Safety: find what could fail before it does, and restrict loads or close a structure when needed. Maintenance planning: catch deterioration early, when repair is cheaper than replacement. Compliance: bridges on public roads are inspected on a federal schedule (see bridge inspection program); many buildings have local or state inspection requirements. Decisions about a change of use, an acquisition or a retrofit: know what you are working with before you design. What an inspector looks for Defects: cracking, spalling, corrosion, section loss, deformation, settlement, water where it shouldn't be. See concrete defects and steel defects. Causes: load, corrosion of reinforcement, freeze thaw, chemical attack, fatigue, poor construction, movement of the foundations. Extent and progression: how much, where, and whether it is getting worse compared with the last inspection. Where NDT fits Most inspection is visual and done with simple tools. Non destructive testing comes in when the question can't be answered from the surface: how deep the cover is, whether the concrete is delaminated, whether the rebar is corroding, how thick the steel still is, whether a weld has a crack inside. See choosing ndt method. Destructive testing (cores, coupons) is used sparingly, to calibrate NDT results or to measure what NDT can only estimate. See concrete cores. What comes out of it A report: what was inspected and how, what was found, the condition ratings, the likely causes, and recommendations with priorities. See inspection reports.

items.s: Initial, routine, in-depth, damage, special, underwater and nonredundant steel tension member inspections, and when each is done.
items.x: In one sentence: the type of inspection sets how close the inspector gets, what tools are used and how often it happens. The types used in bridge practice The U.S. National Bridge Inspection Standards (NBIS) name these types; building owners often use the same ideas. Initial inspection: the first one, when a structure opens or after a major change. It records the baseline: dimensions, materials, condition. Routine inspection: the regular inspection, mostly visual from the deck and the ground, with hand tools. For most highway bridges in the U.S., at least every 24 months , with shorter or longer intervals set by risk (see bridge inspection program). In depth inspection: close up, often hands on, of some or all members, to find defects a routine inspection can't see. May include NDT. Damage inspection: right after an event (vehicle impact, earthquake, fire, flood) to decide whether the structure stays open. Special inspection: follows a known problem at set intervals, such as a crack being monitored or scour at a pier. Underwater inspection: of the parts below water, by divers or other methods. Nonredundant steel tension member (NSTM) inspection: hands on inspection of steel members in tension whose failure could cause collapse, formerly called fracture critical members. Service inspection: a lighter check between routine inspections when the routine interval is extended beyond 48 months. Buildings Building inspections usually follow the purpose: condition assessment before purchase, periodic inspections required by local ordinances (for example balconies and exterior elevated elements, façades, parking structures), and post event safety evaluations. PM notes When you plan an inspection, write down its type and scope first. It tells the team what access, equipment and qualifications to bring.

items.t: How an inspection runs, from desk study to report
items.s: The steps of a structural inspection: records, planning, access, visual inspection, testing, analysis and the report.
items.x: In one sentence: a good inspection is mostly preparation: you arrive knowing the structure, its history and what you're looking for, with the access and the tools to find it. 1. Desk study Gather drawings (original and as built), previous inspection reports and photos, repair records, load ratings and any monitoring data. Note what changed since last time and the defects to follow up. 2. Plan Scope and inspection type (see inspection types). Members to inspect and how close. Tests to run, where and how many. See choosing ndt method. Access: ladders, a lift, an under bridge inspection truck, rope access, a boat, confined space entry. Traffic control and permits for work over or beside a road or railway. Safety plan and the qualifications needed. See ndt certification. 3. Visual inspection Work member by member in a set order, so nothing is missed. Mark defects on drawings or a tablet, measure them, photograph them with a scale, and number them. See visual inspection. 4. Testing Run the planned tests, add tests where the visual inspection found something unexpected, and take cores or samples if needed to calibrate. 5. Analysis Rate the condition (see condition ratings), relate the defects to their likely causes, compare with the last inspection, and decide whether anything needs action now: a load restriction, a closure, temporary shoring. 6. Report Findings, ratings, photos and recommendations with priorities and rough costs. See inspection reports. PM notes Agree with the owner in advance who gets a phone call, and how fast, if the team finds something dangerous on site. Don't wait for the report.

items.t: Concrete defects and what they mean
items.s: Cracks, spalls, delamination, efflorescence, rust staining, scaling and alkali-silica reaction: how to recognize them and what usually causes them.
items.x: In one sentence: most concrete deterioration is water plus something else (salt, carbonation, freezing, reactive aggregate), and the visible defect is usually the last stage of a process that started inside. Cracks Describe each crack by width (with a crack gauge or comparator card), length , orientation , pattern and whether it is active (still moving) or dormant. Plastic shrinkage and drying shrinkage: fine, often random or map like, early in life. Flexural: perpendicular to the span in the tension zone, widest at the face in tension. Shear: diagonal, near supports, a structural concern when wide. Along the reinforcement: often a sign of corrosion pushing the cover off. Map cracking with gel or staining: may point to alkali silica reaction (ASR). Spalls and delamination Delamination: a plane of separation near the surface, usually at the level of the bar, caused by corrosion. It sounds hollow when tapped. See sounding and impact echo. Spall: the delaminated piece has fallen off, often exposing corroded reinforcement. Corrosion of reinforcement Rust staining, cracks along bars and spalls. It starts when chlorides (deicing salt, sea spray) or carbonation reach the steel and break its natural protection. See half cell potential. Surface defects Efflorescence: white deposits where water passes through cracks or joints. Scaling: loss of the surface paste and fine aggregate, often from freeze thaw with salt. Honeycombing: voids from poor consolidation during construction. Abrasion and erosion: wear from traffic or water. Recording Note location, size, quantity (length of cracks, area of spalls and delamination as a share of the element), and photograph with a scale. Element level inspection turns these into condition states. See condition ratings.

items.t: Steel defects: corrosion, fatigue cracks and connections
items.s: Corrosion and section loss, fatigue cracks at details, distortion, and the problems found at bolts, rivets, welds and bearings.
items.x: In one sentence: in steel structures the inspector's attention goes to where water collects, where stress concentrates and where members connect, because that's where section is lost and cracks start. Corrosion and section loss Starts where water and debris collect: under leaking joints, on bottom flanges, at bearings, in pockets of trusses and connections. Record the remaining thickness , not just "heavy rust". Clean a spot, measure with calipers or an ultrasonic thickness gauge (see ultrasonic testing steel), and map the area. Pack rust between plates can pry them apart and break bolts or rivets. Fatigue cracks Repeated loads from traffic make cracks grow from small flaws at stress concentrations: ends of cover plates and attachments welded to flanges; web gaps where cross frames or diaphragms connect; tack welds, intersecting welds, cut outs and holes. Fatigue cracks are tight and hard to see. Clean the area and use magnetic particle dye penetrant or ultrasonic testing to confirm and size them. A crack found in a nonredundant steel tension member needs immediate attention. Connections Missing, loose or broken bolts and rivets. Cracked welds. Bearings that are frozen, tipped, walked off their seats or badly corroded. Distortion Bent or buckled members, often from vehicle impact, fire or overload. Measure the out of straightness and check nearby welds and bolts. Coatings The coating system protects the steel. Record coating condition separately (failure, rust breakthrough) because it predicts where section loss will come next.

items.t: Condition ratings: NBI 0 to 9 and element condition states
items.s: The two rating systems used on U.S. bridges, what each number means, and how they are used to plan work.
items.x: In one sentence: U.S. bridges carry two kinds of rating: a 0 to 9 number for each major component, and condition states 1 to 4 for quantities of each element, and the second is what maintenance plans are built on. Component ratings (0 to 9) The National Bridge Inventory rates the deck , superstructure , substructure and culvert on a scale of 0 to 9: Rating Meaning 9 Excellent 8 Very good 7 Good 6 Satisfactory: minor deterioration 5 Fair: minor section loss, cracking, spalling or scour 4 Poor: advanced section loss, deterioration, spalling or scour 3 Serious: section loss, deterioration or scour seriously affecting primary members 2 Critical: advanced deterioration; may need closing until corrected 1 Imminent failure: major deterioration; closed to traffic, corrective action may restore light service 0 Failed: out of service, beyond corrective action A bridge whose lowest component rating is 4 or less is classified in poor condition; 5 or 6, fair ; 7 or more, good . Poor and fair condition also limit how long the inspection interval can be (see bridge inspection program). Element condition states (1 to 4) Element level inspection, from the AASHTO Manual for Bridge Element Inspection, breaks the bridge into elements (deck, girders, bearings, joints, columns and so on) and records how much of each element is in each state: CS1 Good: no or minor defects. CS2 Fair: moderate defects, no effect on strength. CS3 Poor: defects that need attention. CS4 Severe: defects that may affect strength or serviceability; a structural review may be needed. For example, a deck of 4,000 square feet might be recorded as 3,200 in CS1, 500 in CS2, 250 in CS3 and 50 in CS4. New data specifications The Specifications for the National Bridge Inventory (SNBI), adopted with the 2022 NBIS update, replace the old coding guide, with data collection under the SNBI starting in 2026 through a transition period. Item names and codes change; the idea of rating stays. Using the ratings Component ratings drive federal performance measures and inspection intervals. Element quantities show what to repair and how much, and are the basis for deterioration models in bridge management systems.

items.s: The federal rules for inspecting bridges on public roads: who must inspect, how often, who is qualified and what gets reported.
items.x: In one sentence: every highway bridge over 20 feet on a public road in the U.S. is inspected under the National Bridge Inspection Standards (23 CFR 650, Subpart C), updated in 2022, which set intervals, qualifications and reporting. What the NBIS cover Which bridges: structures carrying public roads with a length over 20 feet, including culverts that size. Who is responsible: each state DOT (Caltrans in California), federal agencies and tribal governments for their bridges, through a bridge inspection organization with a qualified program manager. Who inspects: each inspection team is led by a qualified team leader , a nationally certified bridge inspector who meets the NBIS experience and training requirements. See ndt certification. Intervals (2022 rule) Routine: at least every 24 months by default. Reduced, 12 months or less: for bridges with low ratings or other risk factors, as the rule and the owner's policy set. Extended, up to 48 months: for bridges in good condition meeting set criteria, or by a documented risk based method. Risk based method: a formal assessment can place bridges in categories of 12, 24, 48 or 72 months, but bridges in poor condition can't exceed 24 months, and in fair condition can't exceed 48. Underwater and NSTM inspections have their own intervals; the first ones are due within 12 months of opening. A tolerance of a few months beyond the due date is allowed, depending on the interval. Other requirements Load rating of each bridge and posting of load limits when needed. Procedures for scour critical bridges, NSTMs and complex bridges. Quality control and quality assurance of inspections. Reporting to the National Bridge Inventory, now under the SNBI data specifications. See condition ratings. For consultants Inspection work for an agency follows that agency's manual on top of the NBIS. Read it before the kickoff meeting.

items.s: How to inspect by eye systematically, the simple tools that make it reliable, and the ways to reach the parts of a structure you need to see.
items.x: In one sentence: visual inspection finds most problems, as long as it's systematic, close enough to see, and backed by measurements and photos someone else can follow. Being systematic Follow a fixed order: span by span, element by element, the same direction each time. Use a defect numbering system tied to drawings or a grid. Compare every finding with the previous report: new, same, worse. The basic kit Measuring: tape, folding rule, crack width gauge or comparator card, calipers, level, plumb line. Seeing: flashlight, binoculars, mirror, borescope for cavities and boxes. Probing: hammer for sounding concrete and checking bolts, scraper and wire brush to clean steel, pick. Recording: camera with a scale or ruler in the frame, tablet or field sheets, chalk or crayon to mark defects. Getting close enough Method Good for Ladders Low members, short spans Lifts (boom, scissor) Undersides of short and medium bridges, building façades Under bridge inspection truck Undersides reached from the deck, with traffic control Rope access Tall piers, cable stays, places a vehicle can't reach Boats and divers Piers and foundations in water Drones Overall views and hard to reach surfaces; they find areas to inspect closely, not replace hands on work Confined space entry Box girders, culverts, vaults, with gas monitoring and a permit Recording what you see For every defect: location, type, size (length, width, area, depth), condition state and a photo. A photo without a location and a scale is of little use next time. Safety Fall protection, traffic control, confined space procedures and working over water each need their own plan. On a bridge, the inspector's biggest risk is usually the traffic.

items.s: How the rebound hammer works, what it measures (surface hardness, not strength), and how to use it properly to compare areas of concrete.
items.x: In one sentence: the rebound hammer measures how much a spring driven mass bounces off the concrete surface, which tells you about surface hardness, and with calibration against cores, a rough idea of strength. How it works A spring drives a plunger mass against the concrete. The rebound number is read on a scale or a digital display. Harder, stronger concrete gives a higher rebound. The test is standardized in ASTM C805 (and EN 12504 2 in Europe). Doing it properly 1. Choose test areas on smooth, flat, clean concrete, away from edges and visible defects. Grind off laitance or coatings with the abrasive stone. 2. Hold the hammer perpendicular to the surface. Note the direction (horizontal, up, down), which changes the reading. 3. Take about 10 to 12 readings per area, at least 25 mm (1 inch) apart, never twice in the same spot. 4. Discard outliers as the standard describes, and report the median or average. What affects the reading Surface texture and moisture (wet concrete reads lower). Carbonation: a carbonated surface is harder and reads higher. Aggregate type, age, and whether a bar or a stone sits right below the plunger. Thin or small members that vibrate under the impact. What it's good for Comparing areas of the same concrete to find weaker zones. Estimating strength only when correlated with cores from the same structure. See concrete cores. Combined with ultrasonic pulse velocity ("SonReb" methods) for a better strength estimate. Its limits It only sees the first few centimeters. A reading never replaces a core when strength matters for a structural decision.

items.s: Sending an ultrasonic pulse through concrete to check uniformity, find voids and cracks, and estimate quality.
items.x: In one sentence: ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV) times a sound pulse traveling through the concrete; good, dense concrete carries it fast, and cracks, voids and poor concrete slow it down. How it works A transmitter and a receiver are pressed against the concrete with a coupling gel. The instrument measures the travel time of the pulse; velocity is the path length divided by the time. Standardized in ASTM C597 . Arrangements Direct: transducers on opposite faces. Best accuracy. Semi direct: on adjacent faces, at a corner. Indirect (surface): both on the same face, at several spacings. Useful for estimating crack depth or a damaged surface layer, but less precise. Reading the results Rough guidance often quoted for normal concrete: Velocity (km/s) Quality Above 4.5 Excellent 3.5 to 4.5 Good 3.0 to 3.5 Doubtful Below 3.0 Poor Treat this as a starting point. Aggregate type, moisture and reinforcement change the velocity, so compare readings within the same structure , on a grid, rather than against a table. Good uses Finding voids, honeycombing and cracked zones inside members. Checking uniformity across a structure or after fire damage. Estimating crack depth with the indirect method. With the rebound hammer and cores, estimating strength. Watch out for Bars along the path: steel carries the pulse faster and makes the concrete look better than it is. Keep the path away from bars running parallel to it. Poor coupling on rough surfaces. Wet concrete reads faster than dry.

items.s: Finding reinforcing bars and measuring the concrete cover with electromagnetic cover meters, before coring, drilling or assessing durability.
items.x: In one sentence: a cover meter uses a magnetic field to locate reinforcing bars under the surface and estimate how deep they are, which tells you about durability and where it's safe to drill or core. How it works The probe creates an electromagnetic field; steel bars change it. The instrument shows when the probe is over a bar and estimates the cover (the concrete depth to the bar). Some instruments also estimate bar diameter. Guidance is in BS 1881 204 and ACI 228.2R. Doing it 1. Calibrate or check the instrument on a known block. 2. Scan in one direction to find the outer layer of bars and mark them. Then scan across them to find the second layer. 3. Record cover at a grid of points; good instruments store a map. 4. Confirm a few points by drilling a small hole or at an existing spall. Why cover matters Durability: too little cover lets chlorides and carbonation reach the steel sooner, which starts corrosion. Compare measured cover with what the drawings and codes required. See half cell potential. Safety when drilling or coring: avoid cutting bars or tendons. See concrete cores. Checking construction: whether bars are where the drawings put them. Limits Accuracy drops with depth (typically good to around 100 mm, about 4 inches) and with closely spaced bars or several layers. Doesn't detect non magnetic reinforcement such as stainless or fiber reinforced bars well. For deep bars, dense reinforcement or post tensioning ducts, use ground penetrating radar.

items.s: How GPR maps reinforcement, tendons, voids and deterioration in concrete, and what the hyperbolas on the screen mean.
items.x: In one sentence: ground penetrating radar (GPR) sends radio pulses into the concrete and records the echoes from anything with different electrical properties: bars, ducts, voids, moisture and layer boundaries. How it works An antenna rolled across the surface sends short pulses of radio energy. Reflections come back from interfaces: steel, plastic ducts, voids, the bottom of a slab, a wet layer. The scan shows depth (from travel time) against distance. A bar crossed at right angles shows as a hyperbola , its peak at the bar's position and depth. Higher frequency antennas (around 1.5 to 2.6 GHz) see shallow targets in fine detail; lower frequencies reach deeper with less detail. Uses Locating reinforcement, tendons and conduits before cutting, coring or anchoring, including multiple layers. Slab and deck thickness. Deck deterioration: on bridge decks, areas where the signal from the top bars is weakened often match corroding, chloride contaminated concrete. ASTM D6087 covers this use. Voids under slabs and behind tunnel linings. Calibration Depth depends on the speed of radar waves in the concrete, which changes with moisture. Calibrate on a known depth (a drilled hole or a bar at a spall), or with the hyperbola fitting the software provides. Limits Wet or salt laden concrete absorbs the signal and reduces depth. Dense top reinforcement can hide what's underneath. Interpreting deterioration needs experience and confirmation with other methods: sounding and impact echo, half cell potential, cores.

items.s: Measuring the probability of active reinforcement corrosion with a half-cell, and the related tests: chlorides, carbonation and resistivity.
items.x: In one sentence: a half cell survey measures the electrical potential of the reinforcement through the concrete; more negative values mean a higher probability that the steel is actively corroding. How it works A reference electrode (the half cell, often copper/copper sulfate) is placed on the wetted concrete surface, and a voltmeter is connected to the reinforcement through a small exposed point. The potential between them is read on a grid. Standardized in ASTM C876 . Reading the results (copper/copper sulfate electrode) Potential (mV) Probability of active corrosion (per ASTM C876) More positive than −200 Greater than 90% chance of no corrosion −200 to −350 Uncertain More negative than −350 Greater than 90% chance of corrosion These thresholds are a guide. Look at gradients on the map: a sharp change between neighboring points shows active corrosion better than a single number. Doing it 1. Locate bars and check continuity between test points (see cover meter rebar locating). 2. Pre wet the surface so the reading is stable. 3. Read on a grid (for example 0.5 to 1 m), and map with contours. Companion tests Chloride content at several depths, from dust samples or cores: how much salt reached the bar level. Carbonation depth: spray phenolphthalein on a fresh break; uncolored concrete is carbonated. Resistivity: low resistivity means corrosion can proceed faster. Corrosion rate with linear polarization instruments, when the rate matters. Limits Coatings, epoxy coated bars, very dry or saturated concrete and cathodic protection all affect readings.

items.s: Finding delaminations by sound: hammer sounding and chain drag on the surface, and impact-echo to measure thickness and find flaws.
items.x: In one sentence: delaminated concrete sounds hollow when struck; a hammer or a dragged chain finds it quickly, and impact echo uses the same idea with instruments to measure thickness and find hidden flaws. Hammer sounding Tap the concrete with a hammer; sound concrete rings, delaminated concrete gives a dull, hollow sound. Mark the boundary of each hollow area with chalk and measure it. It's the most common test on soffits, columns and walls. Chain drag On bridge decks and slabs, drag a set of chains across the surface and listen. Hollow areas sound different. ASTM D4580 describes sounding of bridge decks. Traffic noise and asphalt overlays make it harder. Impact echo A small steel ball or impactor strikes the surface, sending a stress wave into the concrete. A transducer next to it records the waves reflecting between the surface and the back of the member, or a flaw. The frequency of the reflections gives the depth: a shallow delamination returns a different frequency than the full thickness. Standardized in ASTM C1383 for thickness measurement. Uses: Thickness of slabs, walls and tunnel linings from one side. Delaminations and voids , including in grouted post tensioning ducts. Scanning versions roll along the surface and map a deck quickly. Related methods Impulse response (ASTM C1740): a hammer with a load cell and a velocity sensor; finds areas of poor support or delamination over larger areas. Infrared thermography: delaminations heat and cool differently from sound concrete in the sun. PM notes Sounding is cheap and quick. Use it first, then instruments where the sound is ambiguous or the deck is overlaid.

items.s: When to take cores, how many, how they are tested for strength, and what else a core can show.
items.x: In one sentence: a core is the reference: a sample of the actual concrete, tested in a lab for strength and examined for what's inside, used to calibrate the non destructive methods. When to core When strength matters for a structural decision: load rating, change of use, retrofit design. To calibrate rebound hammer and ultrasonic pulse velocity results. To see what's inside: depth of cracks, carbonation, delamination planes, chloride profile, reactive aggregate. Planning Locate bars first (see cover meter rebar locating and ground penetrating radar) and avoid cutting them, and never cut post tensioning tendons. Core where stresses are low and the structure can spare it; the engineer of record should agree on locations. Diameter at least about 3 times the maximum aggregate size; 100 mm (4 inch) is common. Enough cores for a statistical result: often at least three per area of concrete being assessed. Testing strength ASTM C42 covers obtaining and testing drilled cores: conditioning, trimming the ends, capping, and correcting for the length to diameter ratio. Core strength is usually lower than the strength of standard cylinders made from the same concrete, and codes such as ACI 318 and ACI 562 say how to judge it. Other things a core shows Depth of carbonation (phenolphthalein). Chloride content at different depths. Petrographic examination for alkali silica reaction, freeze thaw damage, air content. Thickness and layering. After coring Fill the hole with a suitable repair mortar, label each core with location and orientation, and photograph it before it goes to the lab.

items.t: Ultrasonic testing of steel and welds
items.s: Measuring remaining thickness with an ultrasonic gauge and finding flaws inside welds and plates with pulse-echo and phased-array testing.
items.x: In one sentence: ultrasonic testing (UT) sends high frequency sound into steel and reads the echoes, to measure how thick the steel still is or to find flaws inside welds and plates. Thickness gauging A straight beam probe on the surface times the echo from the back wall. Thickness = velocity × time ÷ 2. Used to measure remaining section where corrosion has thinned a flange, web or plate. ASTM E797 covers the method. Multiple echo gauges can read through paint. Tips: Calibrate on a block of known thickness of similar steel. Grind away loose rust and scale, and use couplant. Take a grid of readings in corroded areas, not one spot. Flaw detection (pulse echo) Angle beam probes send sound into the weld at an angle. An echo from inside the weld, at a position the geometry says shouldn't reflect, indicates a flaw : a crack, lack of fusion, slag or porosity. The inspector sizes it by the echo and compares with the acceptance criteria of the governing code, such as AWS D1.1 for structural steel or AWS D1.5 for bridges. Phased array (PAUT) and TOFD Phased array uses many small elements fired in sequence to sweep the beam and produce images of the weld cross section. Faster coverage and a permanent record. Time of flight diffraction (TOFD) uses diffracted signals from crack tips to size cracks in height accurately. Limits Needs a trained, certified operator. See ndt certification. Rough surfaces, thin sections and complex geometry make it harder. Doesn't find surface breaking cracks as easily as magnetic particle dye penetrant; the methods complement each other.

items.t: Magnetic particle and dye penetrant testing
items.s: Two simple surface methods for finding cracks in steel: magnetic particle for ferromagnetic steel, dye penetrant for any non-porous material.
items.x: In one sentence: both methods make a crack you can barely see visible: magnetic particles gather where a crack disturbs a magnetic field, and penetrant dye bleeds out of a crack onto a white developer. Magnetic particle testing (MT) 1. Clean the surface (coatings thicker than a little reduce sensitivity). 2. Magnetize the area with a yoke (an electromagnet with two legs) placed across the expected crack direction. 3. Apply fine iron particles, dry powder or a liquid suspension, often visible or fluorescent. 4. Particles gather at leakage fields where a crack interrupts the magnetic flux, showing its line. 5. Repeat with the yoke turned about 90 degrees: MT finds cracks best when they run across the field. Works on ferromagnetic steel only, finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks. Standardized in ASTM E709 and E1444. Dye penetrant testing (PT) 1. Clean and dry the surface thoroughly. 2. Apply a red or fluorescent penetrant and wait the dwell time (often 5 to 30 minutes). 3. Remove the excess from the surface. 4. Apply a thin white developer ; penetrant trapped in cracks bleeds out and shows as red lines or glows under UV light. Works on any non porous material (steel, stainless, aluminum, welds), finds only surface breaking defects. Standardized in ASTM E165 . Uses on structures Confirming and measuring suspected fatigue cracks at welded details. See steel defects. Checking weld toes and repairs. Inspecting after a crack has been arrested with drilled holes, to see whether the crack tip was caught. Limits Both need clean surfaces and good access. Neither tells you how deep a crack goes: use ultrasonic testing steel for that.

items.s: Imaging the inside of welds and concrete with X-rays or gamma rays: what it shows, how it is done, and the radiation safety it requires.
items.x: In one sentence: radiography passes X rays or gamma rays through a part onto a film or a digital detector; denser or thicker material absorbs more, so voids, cracks and hidden objects show up as differences in the image. How it works A source (an X ray tube or a gamma isotope such as iridium 192 or cobalt 60) is placed on one side, a film or digital detector on the other. The image is a shadow of everything along the path. A void, porosity or slag in a weld absorbs less and shows darker on film; a dense inclusion shows lighter. Image quality indicators placed on the part show that the image is sharp enough. Uses Welds: porosity, slag, lack of fusion, cracks oriented along the beam, in pipes, plates and structural welds. Codes like AWS D1.1 and ASME give acceptance criteria. ASTM E94 is a general guide. Concrete: locating bars, tendons and ducts and checking grout in post tensioning ducts, in members thin enough to penetrate. Castings and components. Digital radiography Computed radiography (imaging plates) and direct digital detectors replace film in much field work: faster results, image enhancement and electronic storage. Radiation safety Radiography is the NDT method with the most serious safety requirements: Only licensed operators and radiation safety officers, under a state radioactive material or X ray license. A controlled exclusion zone with barriers, signs and survey meters, often at night or when the area can be cleared. Personal dosimeters for every radiographer. Secure storage and transport of gamma sources. Limits Cracks show only when they line up with the beam. Access to both sides is needed. Site disruption from the exclusion zone; often UT is chosen instead for welds.

items.s: A question-first guide to picking NDT methods: what you need to know, the material, access, and how methods combine.
items.x: In one sentence: start from the question, not the instrument: decide what you need to know, then pick the cheapest method that answers it, and confirm with a second method or a core where the decision is important. Match the question to the method Question Concrete Steel Is there a hidden delamination or void? sounding and impact echo, ground penetrating radar, thermography — Where are the bars and how deep? cover meter rebar locating, GPR — Is the rebar corroding? half cell potential, chlorides, resistivity — How strong is it? concrete cores, with rebound hammer and ultrasonic pulse velocity for coverage Coupons, hardness Is it uniform, are there internal cracks? UPV, impact echo ultrasonic testing steel How thick is it still? Impact echo, GPR UT thickness gauge Is there a surface crack? Visual, crack gauge magnetic particle dye penetrant What's inside the weld? — UT, phased array, industrial radiography Is it moving or changing? structural health monitoring Monitoring Other factors Access: one side or two? Hands on or from a distance? Surface: coatings, overlays, wet surfaces. Size of the area: spot checks or a whole deck. Scanning methods (GPR, impact echo scanners, thermography) cover large areas quickly. Disruption: traffic control, radiation exclusion zones, noise. Budget and time. Combine methods No single NDT method is decisive. A typical deck survey combines sounding or impact echo (delamination), GPR (cover and deterioration), half cell (corrosion) and a few cores (chlorides and calibration). When methods agree, the conclusion is solid; when they disagree, you've found where to look more closely. Plan the locations Use the visual inspection and the drawings to put tests where the question is: in the defective zone and in a sound zone for comparison.

items.s: Sensors left on a structure to measure movement, strain, cracks, vibration and environment over time, and how monitoring complements inspection.
items.x: In one sentence: inspection is a snapshot; monitoring measures the structure continuously or at set intervals, so you see whether a crack is growing, a support is settling or the structure responds differently than it should. When to monitor A defect whose progression decides the action: a crack, settlement, tilt. During nearby works : excavation, tunneling, pile driving, demolition. After a repair or strengthening , to check it works. On structures of high importance or with uncertain behavior , to support load ratings or extend service life. Common sensors Measures Sensors Crack opening Crack meters (vibrating wire, potentiometric), demountable gauges Strain Vibrating wire or foil strain gauges, fiber optic sensors (FBG, distributed) Tilt and rotation Tiltmeters, inclinometers Displacement and settlement LVDTs, laser and total station surveys, GNSS, leveling Vibration and dynamic response Accelerometers Environment Temperature, humidity, wind, water level Corrosion Embedded corrosion sensors The system Sensors connect to a data logger on site, powered by mains, solar or batteries, which sends data by cellular link to a database and dashboard. Thresholds (alert and alarm levels) send notices when a reading passes them. Always record temperature : most structures move with it, and that movement must be separated from real change. Making it useful Define the question and thresholds before installing. Take a baseline before the event or works you're watching. Check sensors are working: a flat line can mean a stable structure or a dead sensor. Combine with periodic visual inspection. Digital twins Monitoring data can feed a model of the structure (a digital twin) that compares measured and predicted behavior. It's useful when the model is calibrated and someone acts on the differences.

items.s: What an inspection report contains, how to present defects and test results so they can be compared next time, and how to write recommendations owners act on.
items.x: In one sentence: the report is the product: it must let the owner decide what to do, and let the next inspector find and compare every defect you recorded. Structure 1. Summary: overall condition, urgent findings, main recommendations. One page an owner can read alone. 2. Scope and methods: structure, inspection type, date, team, access, tests run and the standards followed, limitations (what couldn't be inspected and why). 3. Description of the structure: type, materials, dimensions, history. 4. Findings by element: defects with location, size, condition state and photo references; comparison with the previous inspection. 5. Test results: tables and maps (cover, potentials, delamination, thickness), with interpretation. 6. Condition ratings. See condition ratings. 7. Assessment: likely causes, rate of deterioration, structural significance. 8. Recommendations: each with a priority, a timeframe and, where possible, an order of magnitude cost. 9. Appendices: defect sheets, photo log, drawings marked with defect locations, instrument calibration records. Recommendations owners act on Priority Typical timeframe Example Urgent Immediately or within days Load restriction, barrier, temporary shoring High Within a year Repair of spalls with exposed corroded bars Medium Within a few years Joint replacement, coating repair Monitor At next inspection Crack to be measured again Be specific: "Repair 12 square feet of spalled concrete at pier 2, south face, with exposed bars", not "Repair concrete as needed". Photos Number every photo, give it a caption with location and what it shows, and include a scale. Take an overview photo before the close up. Words to avoid "Minor", "some", "appears" without measurements. Every qualitative word should come with a number.

items.t: Who may inspect and test: qualifications
items.s: The qualifications for bridge inspectors, NDT technicians and special inspectors, and why they matter for a report to be accepted.
items.x: In one sentence: inspection and test results are only as good as the people who produced them, so owners and codes require specific qualifications for each role. Bridge inspection (NBIS) Team leader: must meet the NBIS qualifications, including completing FHWA approved bridge inspection training and being nationally certified as a bridge inspector, with required experience. Each inspection must be led by one. Program manager: a registered professional engineer or meets the experience and training requirements of the rule. Underwater bridge inspection divers and NSTM inspections have specific training requirements. Refresher training at set intervals. See bridge inspection program. NDT technicians NDT certification is by method (UT, MT, PT, RT and others) and by level: Level I: performs specific tests under supervision. Level II: sets up and calibrates equipment, performs and interprets tests, reports results. Level III: develops procedures, interprets codes, trains and certifies others. Common schemes: the employer based ASNT SNT TC 1A recommended practice, the ANSI/ASNT CP 189 standard, and central certification such as ASNT ACCP or ISO 9712 (common outside the U.S.). Welding inspection often requires an AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) . Concrete testing and special inspection ACI certifications cover field and laboratory concrete testing. ICC special inspector certifications cover inspection during construction required by the building code. Laboratories are often accredited (AASHTO re:source, IAS, A2LA). Engineers Interpreting results, assessing structural capacity and recommending repairs usually falls to a licensed professional engineer, often a structural engineer for complex structures. In California, the Board for Professional Engineers, Land Surveyors and Geologists licenses them. Radiation Radiographers need training and a license holder's authorization under state radiation control rules. See industrial radiography.

items.t: What Procore is and who it is for
items.s: The construction management platform in plain words: the tools, who uses them, and which ones a small electrical GC actually needs.
items.x: In one sentence: Procore is a cloud platform where the owner, the general contractor and the subs keep a project's documents, communication and money in one place, used from a browser in the office and an app in the field. How it is organized Procore is organized as tools : each one handles one kind of record. There are company level tools (the company directory, permissions, templates, company reports) and project level tools (everything about one job). A company turns on the project tools it uses. The tools an electrical GC meets first Where Tools What they replace Field Daily Log, Photos, Timesheets, Inspections, Observations, Punch List Paper dailies, phone photos, timecards, checklists Documents Drawings, Specifications, Documents Plan sets on a shared drive, the spec book PDF Office RFIs, Submittals, Correspondence, Meetings, Schedule Email chains and spreadsheets logs Money Budget, Prime Contracts, Commitments, Change Events, Change Orders, Invoicing Excel budgets, change order logs, pay applications Who logs in Your office: the PM, project engineer and accounting. Your field: foremen and superintendents, mostly from the phone app. Collaborators: subcontractors, suppliers, and sometimes the agency and its engineer. Collaborators usually see only what you share with them. On Caltrans jobs the Resident Engineer works in Caltrans' own systems and forms, so Procore is mainly your system of record: you produce from it the RFIs, submittals, daily reports and change documents Caltrans asks for. See what a caltrans electrical contractor does. What this guide is A practical, independent guide written from Procore's public documentation and from how a Caltrans electrical job runs. Procore changes often: when a screen looks different from what is described here, Procore's own help pages win. In Procore's own help Procore Support. items.t: Is Procore worth it for a small electrical GC?
items.s: When Procore pays off, when a lighter setup is enough, and the questions to answer before you decide.
items.x: In one sentence: Procore pays off when the paperwork of your jobs, not the field work, is what slows you down, and when someone in the company will own the setup. Signs it will pay off Several jobs at once, with RFIs, submittals and changes tracked in separate spreadsheets that drift apart. Documentation disputes: you've lost money on a change or a delay because the daily reports or photos didn't back you up. Field office gaps: the office learns about a problem days after the crew found it. Plan revisions reaching the field late, and work built to an old sheet. Growth: more crews, more subs, larger contracts. Signs a lighter setup is enough, for now One or two jobs at a time and a PM who already keeps tight logs. No one with time to set up templates, cost codes and permissions. A crew that won't use a phone app yet: a platform no one fills in is worse than a good paper form. The real costs besides the subscription Setup time: company directory, permission templates, cost codes, templates for inspections and dailies. Training: office first, then foremen. Process change: one way of doing RFIs, submittals and dailies, used every day by everyone. Integrations with accounting or payroll, if you want them. See procore integrations. Questions to answer before deciding 1. Which three problems do we want to fix first? Write them down. 2. Who will own Procore in the company (setup, training, keeping it clean)? 3. Which tools do we need in the first 90 days? See procore rollout plan. 4. What will we stop doing (spreadsheets, paper forms) once it is running? A trial on one job If you can, run a real job with the first tools: daily log, photos, RFIs, submittals. Judge it by whether the RE got better documents faster, not by how many features you tried. The company directory Add your employees and the companies you work with: suppliers, subs, the agency's people if they'll be invited. Each person is a contact; each person who logs in is a user with a permissions template. Permission templates Procore gives each tool a permission level: None , Read Only , Standard or Admin , with extra granular permissions on some tools. A permissions template bundles those levels for a role, so you assign a role, not 40 settings. Templates can be global (any project) or project specific . items.s: Uploading plan sets and revisions, keeping the field on the current sheet, and handling Caltrans specification books.
items.x: In one sentence: the Drawings tool keeps one current set with every revision behind it, and the Specifications tool splits a spec book into sections, so the crew opens the right sheet and the right section from the phone. Drawings Upload the plan set as PDF. Procore's OCR reads each sheet's number, title and discipline and splits the set into sheets; you review and correct before publishing. When an addendum or a revision arrives, upload it as a revision: the new sheet becomes current and the old one stays in the history. Drawing areas separate sheets that share numbers (for example two interchanges in one contract). Markups and links: draw on a sheet, pin an RFI, a photo or a punch item to a location. Compare two revisions to see what changed before you build. Caltrans electrical sheets (E sheets, standard plans references, pole and conduit schedules) read well when the PDF is clean and vector based; scanned sets need more manual correction. Specifications Upload the spec book as one PDF . Procore uses the text to split it into sections , which you review and publish. Procore groups sections into divisions by matching the first digits of the section number to standard construction codes. Caltrans Standard Specifications and Special Provisions are numbered by Caltrans section (for example Section 86, Electrical Systems), not by the usual building divisions, so expect to check and fix the grouping by hand the first time. When a revised section is uploaded, Procore keeps it as a revision. In the field The app shows the current set and can keep viewed sheets for offline use. See procore field crew onboarding. PM notes Make "publish the revision" part of the same day you receive an addendum. A revision sitting in an email is the most common reason work gets built to an old sheet. items.t: Bringing your field crew on board
items.s: What each foreman needs to learn first, how the app works with poor signal, and how to get daily use instead of end-of-week catch-up.
items.x: In one sentence: the crew needs three things on day one (find the current drawing, take located photos, fill the daily log) and everything else can wait until those are habits. Week 1: three tasks 1. Open the current drawing and find a sheet by number. 2. Take photos in the app so they land in the project, with a location. 3. Fill the daily log : manpower, equipment, notes, delays. See procore daily log. Weeks 2 to 4 Create an observation or punch item from a photo. Fill a checklist (trench, pull box, pre pour). Enter crew hours in Timesheets if you use it. See procore timesheets. Working with poor signal Freeway shoulders, tunnels and remote cabinets often have no signal. According to Procore's help pages, the mobile app keeps items you viewed while online and lets you create many items offline; they sync when the connection returns. So: Before leaving for a remote site, open the drawings, specs and checklists you'll need. Don't delete and reinstall the app in the field: Procore notes that you lose cached items. Check that the day's entries synced before the end of the shift. Making it stick One owner per crew for the daily log, every day, before leaving the site. The PM reads the log every morning and answers. Crews keep filling a log someone reads. Short, phone sized checklists. Long ones get skipped. items.t: The Daily Log and Caltrans daily reports
items.s: How the Daily Log sections map to what a Caltrans daily report must show, and how to avoid entering the same day twice.
items.x: In one sentence: the Daily Log is one shared log per day that the crew fills section by section, and set up right, it gives you everything a Caltrans daily report needs. The sections The Daily Log is organized in sections, many on by default: weather, manpower, notes, timecards, equipment, visitors, phone calls, inspections, deliveries, safety violations, accidents, quantities, productivity, scheduled work, photos, and delays among others. Weather can be filled automatically for the project's location. Admins choose which sections show and in what order. Mapping to a Caltrans daily report What the RE needs Daily Log section Labor by classification and hours Manpower (or Timecards, fed from Timesheets) Equipment on site and hours Equipment Work performed, by location and bid item Notes, Quantities Weather and its effect Weather / Observed weather conditions Delays and their cause Delays Safety meeting, incidents Safety violations, Accidents, Notes Materials delivered Deliveries Photos Photos Visitors, inspectors Visitors, Inspections See daily reports for what a good Caltrans daily report contains. One entry, not two If the crew enters hours in Timesheets , Procore can fill the Daily Log's Timecards from them, instead of typing hours twice. Agree on one output for the RE: a PDF report from Procore, or your own form filled from it. Don't keep a paper daily alongside. Good daily log habits Write delays the day they happen, with the cause and who was told. Name locations the way the plans do (station, pole number, pull box number). Attach photos to the entry they explain. The superintendent or PM reviews and completes the day. PM notes The daily log is your evidence in every change and claim. Write it as if a stranger will read it a year from now. See public works claims. In Procore's own help Daily Log overview. Procore's help pages are the reference for how each screen works today.

items.s: Taking and organizing job photos in Procore so underground work, before-and-after conditions and changes can be found and proven.
items.x: In one sentence: a photo is evidence only if you can find it later and say where and when it was taken, so organize photos by location and phase from day one. What to photograph on an electrical job Before work: existing conditions, damage, utilities, the condition of what you'll touch. Underground before backfill: conduit runs, depth with a tape in the frame, bends, warning tape, tracer wire, bedding. Once it's buried, the photo is all you have. See trenching vs boring. Pull boxes and foundations before and after concrete. Conflicts: anything that becomes an RFI or a change. Installed equipment with labels and serial numbers. Organizing in Procore Use the app's camera so photos land in the project with date and time. Put photos in albums that follow your locations or phases (for example "Phase 2 – Underground – Sta 10+00 to 20+00"). Add a short description : what, where, why. Link photos to the record they support: the daily log entry, the RFI, the observation, the drawing location. Good photo habits A wide shot first, then the close up. Something for scale: a tape, a person, a known object. The location in the frame or the description: station, pole, box number. Several photos of buried work from different angles. PM notes When a change or claim comes up, you'll search photos by location and date. Agree on the album names before the job starts. In Procore's own help Procore Support. items.t: Timesheets, crew hours and certified payroll
items.s: Entering crew hours by cost code and classification in Procore, and what still has to happen in payroll to produce certified payroll.
items.x: In one sentence: Timesheets captures who worked, how long and on what, from the field every day; certified payroll is still produced by your payroll system or a certified payroll tool from those hours. What the Timesheets tool does According to Procore's documentation, the Timesheets tool lets the field enter time for individuals or whole crews on mobile and web, against cost codes , with approvals, and export it to payroll or an ERP. Workers come from the company directory and the Crews tool. Hours can also fill the Daily Log's Timecards section. Setting it up for public works Classifications: make sure each entry carries the worker's prevailing wage classification for the work done (for example inside wireman, laborer, operator), not just their name. On public works the rate depends on the work performed. See prevailing wage. Split days: a worker who pulls wire in the morning and trenches in the afternoon needs two lines. Straight time and overtime recorded separately. Cost codes matching bid items, so labor cost by item is real. Certified payroll Procore Timesheets is time capture, not a certified payroll system. California certified payroll still has to be produced with the right rates and fringes and filed electronically with DIR. Options: export hours to your payroll provider and produce certified payroll there; use a certified payroll or labor compliance application connected to Procore (several are listed in Procore's App Marketplace). See certified payroll and procore integrations. Approvals The foreman enters, the superintendent or PM approves, payroll exports. Hours approved the same week are far more accurate than hours rebuilt at month end. In Procore's own help Timesheets. Procore's help pages are the reference for how each screen works today.

items.s: Checklists for trenches, pull boxes, foundations and pre-energization, and turning a failed item into an observation someone must fix.
items.x: In one sentence: an inspection is a checklist you fill on site; an observation is an issue assigned to someone to fix; a failed checklist item should become an observation. Inspections Built from templates : company level ones you reuse on every project, project level ones for special cases. Each item is answered (for example pass, fail, not applicable), with notes and photos. Best done on the phone, on site, as the work is checked. Observations An issue with a description, location, photos, a type (quality, safety, and so on), an assignee and a due date. Created from an inspection's failed item (it keeps a link to the inspection), from a photo, from a drawing location, or on its own. The assignee responds, the creator verifies and closes. Checklists worth building for electrical work Checklist Examples of items Trench before backfill Depth and cover, conduit type and size, bends, separation, warning tape, tracer wire, bedding Pull box set Type and size, grade, location vs plans, grounding, conduit entries, lid marking Foundation before pour Anchor bolts and template, conduits, rebar, dimensions, approved mix Pre energization Megger and continuity results, labeling, grounding, torque, panel schedule Daily safety walk Traffic control, trench protection, PPE, housekeeping Use the specification's acceptance criteria and your quality plan for the item wording. See electrical testing and grounding and bonding. PM notes Checklists are proof that work was checked before it was covered. Keep them short enough to be filled every time. items.s: The RFI workflow in Procore: RFI manager, assignees, ball in court, official response, and how it fits Caltrans RFI practice.
items.x: In one sentence: in Procore an RFI has an RFI manager who owns it, assignees who answer, and a "ball in court" that always shows who has to act next. The roles Creator: usually your project engineer or a foreman drafting from the field. RFI manager: the person responsible for the RFI through its life; reviews drafts, assigns them, picks the official response, closes. Assignees: the people asked to answer. While an assignee owes a response, they are ball in court ; after they respond, the ball returns to the RFI manager. Distribution list: people kept informed. Official response An RFI can collect several responses. The RFI manager marks the one that answers the question as the official response , then closes the RFI or starts a change event if the answer changes the work. See procore change events. On a Caltrans job The question goes to the Resident Engineer , who usually answers outside Procore, by letter or email in Caltrans' own format. Practical setup: Keep your RFI log in Procore : number, question, references, dates, status, answer. Send the RFI to the RE in the form the contract or the RE asks for (Procore can produce a PDF). When the answer comes back, record it as the official response and attach the RE's document. Assignees can be internal (your PM reviewing a foreman's question) or a designer if the agency allows direct contact. What makes a good RFI doesn't change: one question, references, a proposed solution, the impact and the date you need the answer. See rfis. Useful habits Create RFIs from a drawing markup so the location is attached. Set a due date that reflects the schedule, not a default. Review the open RFIs list in the weekly meeting by ball in court. In Procore's own help Respond to an RFI. Procore's help pages are the reference for how each screen works today.

items.s: Building the submittal register from the special provisions, workflows and ball in court, revisions, and how to keep pace with the RE.
items.x: In one sentence: the Submittals tool holds the register (every item the contract asks you to submit) and routes each submittal through a workflow of reviewers, with revisions kept together. Building the register Procore can scan an uploaded spec book and propose a register (its Submittal Builder ). On Caltrans jobs, check the result against the Special Provisions and the Standard Specifications sections they invoke: Caltrans books don't follow the building industry structure the tool expects. See procore drawings specs. Or import the register from a spreadsheet you already build at the start of the job. Group related items in submittal packages (for example all signal equipment). Numbering can be prefixed by the spec section. The workflow Submittal manager: owns the submittal. Workflow: submitters (often the sub or supplier) and approvers in steps, with due dates. Ball in court follows the current step; when the workflow ends it returns to the submittal manager. Responses such as approved, approved as noted, revise and resubmit, rejected. A revision is created when the reviewer asks for a resubmittal; history stays on one record. On a Caltrans job The RE (or the agency's reviewer) is the final reviewer and usually works outside Procore. A common setup: the supplier submits in Procore, your PM reviews and stamps, you send the package to the RE, and you record the RE's response and attach it. See submittals for what Caltrans expects in an electrical submittal. Keeping pace Track required on site dates for long lead items, not just submission dates. See procurement long lead. Review the list weekly by ball in court. Never release an order on an item that isn't approved. In Procore's own help Submittals best practices. items.s: From a field conflict to a contract change order in Procore: change events, quotes from subs, potential change orders and the tiers.
items.x: In one sentence: a change event records anything that may change scope or cost, before it becomes a change order, so every possible change is tracked, priced and either approved or dropped. The pieces Change event: the record of a possible change: what happened, why, the estimated cost and schedule impact. It can start from an RFI, an observation or a field note. RFQ (request for quote): sent from the change event to a sub or supplier to price their part. Prime contract change order: the change with the owner (for you, Caltrans). Commitment change order: the change with a sub or supplier, on their subcontract or purchase order. Potential change order (PCO): in the two and three tier setups, a step before the change order is final. Procore lets a company choose one, two or three tiers for its change order workflow; fewer tiers means fewer steps between the event and the signed change. On a Caltrans job Caltrans issues Contract Change Orders , and the Standard Specifications set strict notice rules: give written notice when you believe something is extra work, and follow the protest steps if the RE disagrees. Procore helps you track and price; it doesn't replace the contract's notices. See change orders and public works claims. A practical flow: 1. Field finds a conflict → RFI and photos. 2. Answer changes the work → change event the same day, with a note of when you gave the RE written notice. 3. Track costs on that event (labor, equipment, material) or price it with RFQs. 4. Caltrans issues the CCO → record it as a prime contract change order linked to the event. 5. Issue commitment change orders to the subs involved. Reporting The change events log shows open exposure by status: what's pending, priced, approved, rejected. Review it with the budget every month. See procore budget commitments. In Procore's own help Change Events. Procore's help pages are the reference for how each screen works today.

items.s: Setting up the budget by bid item, writing subcontracts and purchase orders as commitments, and reading budget versus cost each month.
items.x: In one sentence: the budget shows what each bid item was expected to cost, commitments show what you've agreed to pay subs and suppliers, and together they show where the job is heading before the money is spent. Budget Built from budget codes in Procore's work breakdown structure (cost code plus cost type such as labor, material, equipment, subcontract). On a Caltrans job, one code per bid item (or group) keeps the budget aligned with the bid and with billing. See procore company setup and bid package. Loaded by hand or imported from a template. Budget changes move money between lines without changing the contract total. Commitments Subcontracts and purchase orders , each with its own schedule of values. Subs can be invited to submit invoices against their commitment. See procore progress billing. Commitment change orders adjust them. See procore change events. Direct costs Costs not tied to a commitment, such as small purchases or your own labor and equipment if they don't come from an integration. Reading the budget each month Column Question it answers Original budget What did we bid? Approved changes What has the agency added or removed? Committed What have we agreed to pay others? Actual / direct costs What has been spent? Forecast to complete What will it take to finish? Projected over/under Where are we heading? PM notes Update the forecast every month. A budget that shows only what was spent tells you about the past; the forecast is what helps you act. In Procore's own help Financial management guide: specialty contractor. items.s: Owner invoices and subcontractor invoices in Procore, retention, and how to line them up with Caltrans progress estimates.
items.x: In one sentence: Procore's Invoicing tool builds your monthly bill to the owner from the prime contract's schedule of values and collects your subs' invoices against their commitments, with retention on both. Owner invoices Built from the prime contract's schedule of values : work completed this period, materials stored, retention. On a unit price Caltrans job, the SOV lines follow the bid items and quantities. Approved prime contract change orders appear as lines once executed. Subcontractor invoices Subs (as invoice contacts) submit against their subcontract's schedule of values , or you create the invoice on their behalf. You review, approve or return for revision. Retention can be set and released per line; Procore also supports sliding scale retention. Lining up with Caltrans Caltrans pays from the RE's monthly progress estimate , based on quantities the inspector measures, not from your invoice. So: 1. Track quantities weekly with the inspector. 2. Build your owner invoice in Procore from the same quantities, as your internal record. 3. When the RE's estimate arrives, compare line by line and resolve differences. 4. Pay subs their share within the time state law requires once you're paid. See prompt payment subcontractors. Retention on California public works is generally capped at 5%, and the prime can't hold more from subs than the agency holds from it. See progress payments retention. Supporting documents Keep certified payroll, lien releases and insurance current for each sub; many GCs require them before approving a sub invoice. Procore has compliance features for this, and Procore Pay adds payment and lien waiver handling where it's used. In Procore's own help Invoicing. items.s: Keeping meeting minutes, letters to the RE, notices and the schedule in Procore so the record is complete and searchable.
items.x: In one sentence: the formal record of a job is more than RFIs and submittals: meeting minutes, letters, notices and the schedule belong in the same place so you can find them when it matters. Meetings Agenda, attendees, minutes and action items with owners and due dates. Recurring series for the weekly meeting with the RE and the internal coordination meeting. Action items carried forward until closed. Typical Caltrans meetings to record: the preconstruction meeting, weekly progress meetings, safety meetings, and meetings with utility companies. Correspondence Procore offers a Correspondence tool for formal communication types your company defines, for example: letters to and from the RE; notices of potential extra work, delay or differing site conditions; transmittals. Each type gets its own numbered log. Notices are where deadlines live: record the date sent and how it was sent. See public works claims. Schedule Upload or connect the baseline schedule and its updates so the team sees the current one. Caltrans contracts set schedule submission requirements in the special provisions; keep each submitted version and the RE's response. Email Forward important emails into the project record. An answer that lives only in someone's inbox is lost when that person leaves. PM notes If it would matter in a dispute, it goes in the project record the day it happens. items.s: Punch items with a punch item manager, assignees and a final approver, created from the phone and closed with photos.
items.x: In one sentence: each punch item is a location, a description, a photo, a responsible party and a due date, and it closes only when someone verifies the fix. The roles Punch item manager: oversees the item, assigns it and forwards it for final approval. Assignees: do the work and mark it ready for review. Final approver: has the authority to close the item; often its creator. Statuses track each step, for example work required, ready for review, work not accepted, ready to close and closed. On a Caltrans job The RE's punch list arrives as a list or a walk through. Practical use: 1. Enter each item in Procore from the phone during the walk, with a photo and a pin on the drawing . 2. Assign it to your crew or the responsible sub with a due date. 3. The crew fixes it and adds an "after" photo. 4. Your superintendent verifies and closes; you report back to the RE in the format they want. Items can be created offline in the app and sync later. Punch list types Create types (electrical, civil, signing and striping, landscaping) so you can sort by trade and send each sub only its items. PM notes Start a running "pre punch" list a few weeks before completion. The RE's punch list is shorter when you've walked the job first. See acceptance testing punch list. items.t: Building the closeout package as you go

See procore records export. PM notes Make closeout documents a condition of a sub's retention release. They're easiest to get while the sub still wants to be paid. items.t: Keeping your records after the job
items.s: What to export from Procore at closeout and before a subscription changes, and how to keep it for audits and claims.
items.x: In one sentence: your project records must outlive the job and your software, so export a complete archive at closeout and keep it under your company's control. Why it matters on public works Labor compliance audits can come after the job is closed. See labor compliance penalties. Claims, warranty issues and agency audits can arise years later. Contracts and the law set record retention periods; follow the longest that applies. What to export Daily logs (with photos). RFIs and submittals with all responses and attachments. Change events and change orders. Drawings: the final current set and the revision history. Meeting minutes and correspondence. Inspections, observations and punch list. Financial records: budget, commitments, invoices (also in your accounting system). How According to Procore's help pages, the project archive tool (renamed from Data Extracts 2.0) exports data from several tools into an organized download, most items as PDF and files in their original format; an archive is available to download for 30 days after it's created. An older Windows application, Procore Extracts, also exports a project's data to folders on a computer. Check which one your account has. Storing it Company storage you control, with a backup. A consistent folder name: contract number, route, year. A short index of what's inside and when it was exported. Before you sign or renew Ask how you export your data and what happens to it if you leave. See procore questions before signing. items.s: An adoption order for a small electrical GC: which tools first, who learns what, and how to know it is working.
items.x: In one sentence: roll out in three waves (field record first, then the office logs, then money), and only start the next wave when the previous one is used every day. Before day 1 Name the internal owner of Procore. Company setup: directory, permission templates, cost codes. See procore company setup. Pick one live job to start. Days 1 to 30: the field record Drawings and specifications current on every phone. See procore drawings specs. Daily log every day. See procore daily log. Photos in the app, in albums. See procore photos. Measure: daily logs completed the same day, percentage of photos in Procore. Days 31 to 60: the office logs RFIs and submittals moved from spreadsheets to Procore. See procore rfis and procore submittals. Meetings and correspondence recorded. Inspections for two or three key checks. Measure: open RFIs and submittals reviewed weekly by ball in court. Days 61 to 90: money Budget by bid item, commitments for subs and suppliers. Change events for every potential change. Monthly owner invoice built in Procore and reconciled with the RE's estimate. Measure: change events opened the day the issue arises. After 90 days Add the second and third jobs with the project template. Decide on Timesheets and integrations. See procore integrations. Retire the old spreadsheets. Signs it isn't working The crew fills logs at the end of the week. Spreadsheets still updated "just in case". Only one person knows how anything works. items.t: Integrations an electrical GC asks about
items.s: Accounting, payroll and certified payroll, scheduling, estimating and storage: what exists in Procore's marketplace and what to check before connecting.

Run the core tools for a few months, then add the one integration that saves the most time, usually accounting or payroll. Whatever tool you use must produce that, and someone must still check it. See certified payroll. In Procore's own help Procore App Marketplace.
