items.s: Sole owner, partnership, corporation or LLC: what each means for liability, taxes, bonds and the contractor license in California.
items.x: In one sentence: the structure decides who is liable, how profit is taxed and what the license costs to hold, so pick it with your CPA before you apply for the license, because changing it later usually means a new license. The four common choices Structure Liability License notes Sole owner The owner is personally liable for everything Simplest license; the owner or an RME qualifies it Partnership Partners are personally liable A general partner or an RME qualifies it Corporation Liability generally stays with the company An RMO (an officer) or an RME qualifies it LLC Liability generally stays with the company Extra bond and liability insurance required What an LLC license adds in California CSLB requires an LLC license to carry, besides the contractor bond, a $100,000 LLC employee/worker bond and liability insurance of at least $1 million, rising with the number of people listed on the license (up to $5 million). Those are recurring costs every year you hold the license. Check CSLB's LLC page for the current amounts. Taxes, briefly A corporation can be taxed as a C corporation or elect S corporation treatment; an LLC can be taxed as a partnership or elect corporate treatment. The choice changes how the owners pay themselves and how much self employment tax they pay. This is a CPA conversation, not a do it yourself one. Questions to answer before choosing 1. How much personal risk can the owners accept? 2. Will there be more than one owner, now or later? 3. Will you bid public works with bonds? Sureties look at the company and usually ask the owners to sign a personal indemnity anyway. See bonding capacity. 4. Do you plan to sell the company or bring in a partner later? PM notes Limited liability does not protect an owner from everything: personal guarantees, indemnity agreements with the surety and some labor claims still reach the owner. Read what you sign. Official sources CSLB: Licenses for limited liability companies · CSLB.

items.t: The license and the qualifier: RMO and RME
items.s: Who qualifies a company's license, the difference between an RMO and an RME, and the 90 days you have when the qualifier leaves.
items.x: In one sentence: a company's license rests on one person, the qualifier, and if that person leaves you have 90 days to replace them before the license is suspended. Who the qualifier is The qualifier is the person listed with CSLB who met the experience and exam requirements for the license classification. Depending on the structure, it can be: the owner of a sole ownership; a qualifying partner ; an RMO (responsible managing officer) of a corporation, or the LLC equivalents (responsible managing member or manager); an RME (responsible managing employee): an employee who qualifies the license. RME rules worth knowing An RME must be a bona fide employee actively involved in the business. CSLB defines this in hours per week; check the current rule before you hire one. An RME can qualify only one active license at a time. When the license is qualified by an RME, a $25,000 bond of qualifying individual is usually required in addition to the $25,000 contractor bond. When the qualifier leaves The company or the qualifier must notify CSLB in writing within 90 days of the departure. The company must replace the qualifier within 90 days . If not, the license is automatically suspended (or the classification removed). One 90 day extension can be requested in limited circumstances, and the request must arrive within the first 90 days. The departing qualifier stays responsible for work done before their recorded departure date. See contractor license classes for the classifications themselves. Protecting the company If the qualifier is not an owner, have a second qualified person in the company or a plan to find one. Put the notice and cooperation duties in the RME's employment agreement. Keep a copy of the license record and check it after any change. Official sources CSLB: Change in personnel · CSLB.

items.s: Bank accounts, bookkeeping, payroll, insurance, document storage and the calendar of renewals that a small contractor needs from day one.
items.x: In one sentence: a contractor's office is a short list of systems (bank, books, payroll, insurance, files and a renewals calendar) that must work every week, whoever is on vacation. The minimum set System What good looks like Bank Business accounts only, separate from personal; a separate account for payroll is common Bookkeeping Construction aware accounting software with jobs and cost codes from day one Payroll A provider that handles California rules, certified payroll if you do public works, and workers' comp reporting Insurance Workers' comp, general liability, auto, equipment; a broker who knows contractors Files One shared, backed up folder structure: company, jobs, people, equipment Renewals calendar License, bonds, insurance, DIR registration, vehicle registrations, certifications Workers' compensation Any contractor with employees must carry workers' compensation insurance. California law also moves toward requiring it for every licensed contractor, with or without employees; the date has been pushed back before, so check CSLB for the current requirement. See insurance for public works for the other policies. Files that outlive people Set up the job folder template once (contract, insurance, submittals, RFIs, change orders, daily reports, photos, billing, closeout) and use it on every job. When someone leaves, the job's history stays. Renewals calendar Put every expiry date in one shared calendar with a reminder 60 days before. A lapsed bond, a lapsed workers' comp policy or a lapsed DIR registration can stop work or a bid. Software, step by step Start with accounting and payroll. Add a field app (daily reports, photos, time) when the paperwork from the field starts slipping. See procore for small gc for how to judge a larger platform. Official sources CSLB: workers' compensation for licensees (B&P 7125).

items.t: Job costing: knowing what each job really made
items.s: Coding every hour and every invoice to a job and a cost code, comparing to the estimate while the job is running, and closing the loop into the next bid.
items.x: In one sentence: job costing means every cost lands on a job and a cost code, so you can compare actual to estimate during the job, not just discover the result at year end. The building blocks Jobs: one per contract (and one for shop or overhead time). Cost codes: the same codes the estimate used, by activity (trenching, conduit, pull boxes, wire, testing) or by bid item on unit price work. Cost types: labor, burden, material, equipment, subcontract, other. Coding costs Labor: time cards by job and cost code every day. A whole day on "general" teaches you nothing. Burden: payroll taxes, workers' comp, benefits; allocated as a percentage of labor or by hour. Material: every supplier invoice coded when it's entered, using the PO. Equipment: owned equipment charged at an internal hourly or daily rate; rentals at cost. Reading the report Column What it tells you Estimate What you bid Cost to date What you've spent Percent complete How much of the work is done (from the field, not from cost) Projected final cost What the job will cost if trends hold Projected margin What you'll actually make The key number is percent complete from the field . Cost to date divided by budget is not progress; it's spending. Closing the loop At the end of each job, compare actual productivity (feet of conduit per crew day, boxes set per day) with the estimate, and update the estimating database. That's how the next bid gets sharper. PM notes Review job cost every two weeks with the foreman. Problems found at 30% complete can be fixed; problems found at closeout can only be explained.

items.t: Overhead and markup: pricing so the company earns money
items.s: Building an overhead budget, turning it into a recovery rate, and adding profit on top so each job pays its share.
items.x: In one sentence: every job must cover its direct costs, its share of the office and yard, and a profit, so you need to know your overhead per year before you can price a job correctly. What overhead is Costs that keep the company running but don't belong to one job: office rent, utilities, phones, software; office salaries (owner, estimator, office manager, PM time not charged to jobs); insurance not charged to jobs, licenses, bonds' annual fees, professional fees; vehicles and tools not charged to jobs; marketing, training, bidding costs. The overhead budget 1. List next year's overhead costs, month by month. 2. Estimate next year's volume of work (revenue or direct cost). 3. Divide: overhead / expected direct cost = the overhead recovery rate to add to every job's direct cost. Example: $400,000 of overhead on an expected $2,000,000 of direct cost means each job needs 20% on top of direct cost just to pay the office. Markup vs margin Markup is added to cost: cost $100 + 25% markup = $125 price. Margin is a share of price: $25 profit on a $125 price is a 20% margin. Mixing the two is one of the most common ways contractors underprice. Profit Profit is not what's left over; it's a line in the price. It pays for growth, bonding capacity, equipment and bad years. When volume drops If the company does less work than planned, overhead per job goes up. That's the moment to cut overhead or find work, not to drop prices below cost. PM notes Know your break even volume : the amount of work at which overhead is just covered. Below it, every month loses money.

items.s: Why profitable contractors run out of money: payroll every week, payment 30 to 60 days later, retention held to the end, and how to forecast and protect cash.
items.x: In one sentence: a contractor pays crews weekly and suppliers monthly but gets paid weeks after billing, minus retention, so a growing, profitable company can still run out of cash. Where the gap comes from 1. Work done in month 1 is billed at the end of month 1. 2. The owner pays 30 days or more later; public agencies follow their own cycles. 3. Retention is held until completion. See progress payments retention. 4. Meanwhile payroll goes out every week and suppliers want 30 days. On a big new job, the gap grows before the first check arrives. A 13 week cash forecast Once a week, update a simple sheet: cash today; expected receipts by week, job by job, with realistic dates; payroll, suppliers, subs, rent, loan payments, taxes by week; the lowest balance in the next 13 weeks. If the lowest point is too close to zero, act now: speed up billing, talk to the bank, delay a purchase. Getting paid faster Bill on time, every month, on the owner's format and with all backup. Track each pay application until it's paid; call on day one of lateness. Settle change orders quickly; unsigned extra work is unbilled cash. See getting paid on changes and closeout. Use prompt payment rights where the law gives them. See prompt payment subcontractors. Paying out wisely Negotiate supplier terms; pay on time to keep them. Pay subs when you're paid, within the law's limits. Don't fund equipment purchases from operating cash; finance them. See credit lines and equipment finance. PM notes Cash problems almost never come from one bad month. They come from billing late, change orders unsigned for months and a job that grew faster than the cash to fund it.

items.t: Financial statements a surety and a bank want to see
items.s: Balance sheet, income statement and the work-in-progress schedule: what they show, why over- and under-billing matter, and what level of CPA work to get.
items.x: In one sentence: sureties and banks judge a contractor on three documents, the balance sheet, the income statement and the work in progress schedule, and on how much a CPA stands behind them. Balance sheet What the company owns and owes on one date. Sureties look hardest at: working capital: current assets minus current liabilities; net worth (equity); receivables that are old or doubtful; debt and who it's owed to. Income statement Revenue, cost of work and overhead over a period. The question is whether the company makes money consistently, and whether gross profit holds up as volume grows. The WIP schedule The work in progress schedule lists every open job: Column Meaning Contract value Including approved changes Estimated total cost Current estimate at completion Cost to date Spent so far Percent complete Cost to date / estimated total cost Earned revenue Contract value × percent complete Billed to date What's been invoiced Over / under billing Billed minus earned Overbilling (billed more than earned) means you have the owner's cash in advance; it's a liability, and too much can hide a losing job. Underbilling (earned more than billed) means you've done work you haven't billed, often unsigned change orders or a job going wrong. Sureties read both closely. Levels of CPA work Compilation: the CPA formats your numbers, no assurance. Review: the CPA does limited checks and gives limited assurance. Audit: full testing and an opinion. Larger bonding programs usually require a review or audit, prepared by a CPA who knows construction and uses percentage of completion accounting. PM notes The WIP schedule is only as good as the estimated costs to complete. Update them honestly every quarter. See job costing.

items.t: Bonding capacity: how it is set and how to grow it
items.s: Single and aggregate limits, what a surety looks at, the personal indemnity, and the steps that grow bonding capacity over time.
items.x: In one sentence: your bonding capacity is the surety's judgment of how much work you can carry at once and on one job, and it grows with working capital, net worth, a track record and good financial reporting. The two limits Single job limit: the largest one contract the surety will bond. Aggregate limit: the total of all your uncompleted bonded (and often unbonded) work at once. What the surety looks at Often summarized as the three Cs: Capital: working capital and net worth on CPA prepared statements. Sureties commonly size capacity as a multiple of working capital; ask your agent what multiple your surety uses. Capacity: your experience with jobs of that size and type, your people and your equipment. Character: reputation, paying suppliers and subs, finishing jobs, honesty with the surety. The indemnity agreement Sureties almost always ask the company and its owners (often spouses too) to sign a general indemnity agreement: if the surety pays a claim, they can recover from you. Read it with an attorney. See surety bonding and payment performance bonds. Growing capacity 1. Keep profit in the company instead of distributing it all; working capital is the base. 2. Get reviewed or audited statements from a construction CPA. See contractor financial statements. 3. Grow job size in steps; a track record on $2 million jobs supports a request for $3 million. 4. Send the surety quarterly WIP schedules without being asked. 5. Keep a bank line of credit; it shows liquidity. 6. Use a surety agent who specializes in contractors. SBA surety bond guarantee Small contractors that can't yet get standard bonding may qualify for the U.S. Small Business Administration's surety bond guarantee program through participating sureties. Check the SBA's current limits. PM notes A surety relationship is long term. Tell them early about a job in trouble; surprises cost more capacity than bad news.

items.t: Credit lines, equipment loans and leasing
items.s: Which kind of financing fits which need: a line of credit for the cash gap, term loans or leases for equipment, and what lenders ask for.
items.x: In one sentence: match the financing to the need: a revolving line of credit for timing gaps between paying and getting paid, and a loan or lease for equipment that lasts years. Line of credit Draw when payroll comes before payment, repay when the payment arrives. Usually secured by receivables and backed by the owners' guarantee. Banks look at the same statements as the surety, plus receivable aging. A line used and repaid regularly is healthy; a line maxed out for months is a warning sign. Equipment loans You own the equipment; the loan is secured by it. Term usually matches the equipment's useful life. Works when the machine will be used steadily for years. Leases Operating lease: closer to a long rental; returned at the end. Finance (capital) lease: works like a loan; you usually own it at the end. Leases can preserve cash and working capital; your CPA can explain how each type shows on your statements, which matters to the surety. Other sources SBA guaranteed loans through banks. Supplier terms (30 to 60 days) are financing too; use them and pay on time. Factoring receivables is expensive and usually a sign of a cash problem. What lenders ask for Financial statements, tax returns, the WIP schedule, receivable aging, a list of equipment, and personal financial statements from the owners. See buy rent or lease equipment for deciding whether to own equipment at all. PM notes Set up the line of credit when you don't need it. Banks lend to companies that look like they won't need the money.

items.s: Where to find electricians, laborers and operators, how to check skills before trusting someone with a job, and what to have ready on their first day.
items.x: In one sentence: hire for safety habits and reliability as much as skills, check the skills on a real task, and have the paperwork, tools and a buddy ready on day one. Where to find people Referrals from your best workers; often the best source. Union hiring halls, if you're signatory. See union or open shop. Trade schools and apprenticeship programs. See apprentices on public works. Suppliers and other contractors who hear who's looking. Job boards, with a clear description of the work, the pay and the location. Checking skills Ask about the specific work: conduit bending, pulling, terminations, trenching, equipment. Ask for certifications that matter: OSHA training, flagger, equipment operator cards, fiber splicing. A short skills check on the first day: bend an offset, terminate a conductor, read a plan sheet. Call a previous foreman, not just the office. Day one New hire paperwork (federal and state tax forms, employment eligibility verification, the California wage notice). Safety orientation and the Code of Safe Practices. See safety program. PPE and tools, signed out. A named crew lead or buddy for the first weeks. The first 30 days Check in at the end of week one and at 30 days: safety, quality, attendance, attitude. Decide early; a poor fit doesn't usually improve on a crew. Pay Know the going rate for each classification in your area. On public works, prevailing wage sets the minimum by classification. See prevailing wage. PM notes Your best recruiting tool is a reputation for paying correctly and on time, safe jobs and steady work.

items.s: What signing a collective bargaining agreement changes for bidding, payroll, hiring and flexibility, and what to ask before you sign.
items.x: In one sentence: signing with a union gives you trained workers from the hall, a set wage and benefit package and access to work that requires it, in exchange for the agreement's rules on pay, hiring and how work is staffed. What changes when you sign Topic Union (signatory) Open shop Hiring Through the hall, under the agreement's rules You recruit directly Pay and benefits Set by the agreement, paid into trust funds You set them, above legal and prevailing minimums Training Apprenticeship through the joint program Your own, or state approved programs Flexibility Work rules, ratios and jurisdiction set by the agreement You decide Market Access to projects with labor agreements Some projects require union labor Project labor agreements Some public projects are built under a project labor agreement (PLA). Open shop contractors can usually bid, but must follow the PLA's terms on that job, such as hiring through the hall and paying into trust funds. Read the PLA before bidding. On public works Prevailing wage applies either way. Union and open shop contractors pay at least the same total rates on public works; the difference is how benefits are provided. See prevailing wage and certified payroll. Questions before signing 1. Which agreement, which local, which classifications and which area? 2. What are the total hourly costs (wages, benefits, training) for each classification? 3. Hiring rules: can you name request your own people? 4. Apprentice ratios and work rules. 5. What happens to your existing employees? 6. How do you leave later, and what liabilities (for example pension withdrawal) could follow? PM notes This is a long term decision. Talk to a labor attorney and to other contractors of your size on both sides.

items.t: Foremen: promoting, training and keeping them
items.s: Why the foreman makes or loses money on a job, how to pick and train one, and how to keep good foremen from leaving.
items.x: In one sentence: the foreman controls productivity, safety and the daily record on every job, so choosing, training and keeping good foremen is one of the highest return things a small contractor does. What a foreman owns Planning tomorrow's work, material and equipment today. The crew: who does what, coaching, discipline. Safety: tailgate meetings, hazards, stopping unsafe work. See safety program. Quality: built to plan and spec the first time. The record: daily reports, hours by cost code, photos, extra work. See daily reports. Communication with the PM, the inspector and other trades. Choosing one The best journeyman isn't always the best foreman. Look for someone who plans ahead, stays calm, writes clearly enough, is respected by the crew and tells you about problems early. Training Reading the estimate: hours and quantities by cost code for their job. Daily reports and time by cost code, and why they matter in a claim. Change recognition: what's extra work, and who to tell before doing it. Leadership basics: giving instructions, correcting, handling conflict. A short job start meeting with the PM on every job: scope, budget, schedule, risks. Keeping them Pay that reflects the responsibility; consider a share of job savings tied to safety and quality, not just speed. Give them the plan, the tools and the material they asked for. Back them up with the inspector and the crew. Ask their opinion on bids and methods. PM notes Show each foreman their job's cost report every two weeks. Foremen who see the numbers start managing them. See job costing.

items.s: Employee or subcontractor, daily overtime, meal and rest breaks, pay records and the notices California requires of construction employers.
items.x: In one sentence: California has stricter wage rules than federal law, with daily overtime, timed meal and rest breaks and strict classification of workers, and construction is one of the most audited industries. Employee or independent contractor California uses the ABC test to decide whether a worker is an employee. In construction, a subcontractor relationship can escape the ABC test only under specific conditions in Labor Code section 2781, including a written subcontract and a subcontractor that holds its own CSLB license and runs its own business. A worker you pay by the job without those conditions is very likely your employee. See the DLSE's independent contractor FAQ. Overtime For construction (IWC Wage Order 16), non exempt workers generally earn: 1.5× the regular rate after 8 hours in a day or 40 in a week; 2× after 12 hours in a day, with special rules for the seventh consecutive day. Prevailing wage jobs have their own overtime rates in the wage determination. See prevailing wage. Meal and rest breaks A paid 10 minute rest break for every 4 hours worked (or major fraction). An unpaid 30 minute meal break when working more than 5 hours, starting no later than the end of the fifth hour; a second one after 10 hours. The first can be waived by mutual consent only if the day is 6 hours or less. A missed break generally costs one hour of pay at the regular rate, per worker, per day. Pay records Itemized wage statements with the required information, accurate time records and payroll records kept for the required period. Give new hires the written wage notice required by Labor Code section 2810.5. Heat Cal/OSHA's heat illness prevention rules apply to outdoor work: water, shade, rest, training and a written plan. PM notes Track time and breaks daily, in the field, not rebuilt at the end of the week. Most wage claims are about time records that can't be proved. Talk to an employment attorney before setting up pay practices. Official sources DIR: construction employer brochure · DLSE: independent contractor vs. employee.

items.t: Safety program as a business system
items.s: The written IIPP and Code of Safe Practices, tailgate meetings every 10 working days, records, and why your experience modification rate affects your bids.
items.x: In one sentence: a safety program is required by law, protects your people and directly affects your insurance cost and whether you can bid, so run it like any other business system: written, trained, checked and recorded. What Cal/OSHA requires of construction employers A written, effective Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) under Title 8, section 3203, as required for construction by section 1509. A written Code of Safe Practices for your operations, posted at the job site office or given to each supervisor. Tailgate or toolbox safety meetings led by supervisors at least every 10 working days . Heat illness prevention for outdoor work, and the specific programs your work needs (trenching, fall protection, electrical safety, traffic control). Running it 1. Assign responsibility: a named person in the office and each foreman in the field. 2. Inspect: job site inspections on a schedule, corrected and recorded. 3. Train: new hires before work starts; refresher and task training; record who, what and when. 4. Investigate: every injury and near miss, to find the cause, not someone to blame. 5. Record: training, meetings, inspections and injury logs, kept where you can find them. Your experience modification rate California's workers' compensation experience modification compares your actual losses with the losses expected for contractors of your type and size. 1.00 (100%) is average; above it usually raises your premium, below it usually lowers it. Many owners and general contractors ask for your mod in prequalification. See prequalification and bid lists. Getting help Cal/OSHA Consultation Services offers free, confidential help separate from enforcement. Your workers' comp insurer usually has loss control staff too. PM notes The best safety metric isn't the injury count; it's whether foremen hold the meetings, inspect and stop unsafe work. Measure those. Official sources Title 8, section 1509 · Cal/OSHA guide to developing your IIPP · WCIRB: experience modification.

items.s: Public or private, prime or sub, which agencies and which job sizes: deciding where a small contractor can win and make money.
items.x: In one sentence: a small contractor makes money by being very good at a narrow kind of work for a known set of customers, so choose your market on purpose instead of bidding everything. Public or private Public works Private work Finding work Published bids, open to all qualified bidders Relationships and invitations Award Usually lowest responsive, responsible bid Price, relationship, reputation Paperwork Heavy: prevailing wage, certified payroll, bonds, submittals Lighter, depends on the owner Payment Slow but sure Varies with the owner's finances See public works basics. Prime or sub As a sub , you deal with one GC, a narrower scope and less paperwork, but the GC controls schedule and payment. As a prime , you deal with the owner directly and control the job, but carry bonding, coordination and all the risk. See from sub to prime. Narrowing down 1. Your strength: which work do you do better and cheaper than others? (Use job cost history, not feelings.) 2. Customers: which agencies, GCs or owners pay well and treat subs fairly? 3. Geography: how far can crews travel and stay profitable? 4. Job size: the range your bonding, cash and crews can carry. 5. Competition: how many bidders show up, and how close are the results? Using bid results Public bid results show who bids, how often and how far apart. Track them for your target agencies to see where you're competitive. See finding public bids. PM notes Write your target market in one sentence and check every bid against it. "Caltrans and city electrical work under $3 million within 60 miles" is a market; "anything electrical" isn't.

items.t: Prequalification and getting on bid lists
items.s: The questionnaires owners and GCs use to decide who may bid, what they ask, and how to keep a ready package so you never miss a deadline.
items.x: In one sentence: many owners and general contractors only invite or accept bidders who prequalified, so keep a ready to send package and fill every questionnaire completely and on time. What prequalification asks Company: legal name, structure, license numbers and classifications, DIR registration, years in business, owners. Financial: statements, bonding capacity letter from your surety, bank reference. Safety: experience modification rate for three years, injury logs, IIPP, safety programs, citations. See safety program. Experience: completed projects with contract values, owners and contacts. Legal: claims, litigation, defaults, debarments, license actions. Insurance: certificates and limits. Some public agencies use formal prequalification for certain projects; many GCs use their own questionnaires or third party systems. Keep a ready package One folder, updated every quarter: company profile and organization chart; license and DIR registration printouts; surety letter (current); insurance certificates; three years of mod rates and injury logs; project list with references; financial statements (sent only where confidentiality is assured). Getting on bid lists Register on agency vendor and plan room sites for your trade. Ask GCs you want to work with how they invite subs, and fill their form. Respond to every invitation, even to decline, so you stay on the list. PM notes A late or half filled questionnaire tells a GC how you'll handle submittals. Treat it like one.

items.t: Building relationships with GCs, agencies and suppliers
items.s: How a small contractor earns repeat work: delivering, communicating early, paying on time, and staying in touch between bids.
items.x: In one sentence: repeat work comes from people who trust you to show up, tell the truth early and finish clean, so every job is also a sales call. With general contractors Submit complete bids on time, with clear scope and exclusions. Hit submittal and schedule dates; GCs remember who held them up. Tell them about problems early, with a proposed solution. Clean closeout: punch list, as builts, O&M manuals without chasing. With agencies and inspectors Professional, complete paperwork: daily reports, certified payroll, submittals. Respect for the inspector's role, even in disagreement. Preconstruction and progress meetings: be prepared, short and factual. With suppliers Pay on time; a supplier who trusts you gives better prices, terms and allocation in a shortage. Share bid schedules early so they can price. Give them feedback on their quotes after the bid. Between jobs After each job, ask the PM or owner what went well and what didn't. Attend industry associations and agency outreach events. Keep a short list of key contacts and talk to each a few times a year. PM notes Reputation is local and fast. One unpaid supplier or one abandoned punch list travels further than ten good jobs.

items.t: Saying no: which jobs to pass on
items.s: A bid/no-bid checklist: fit with your market, capacity, risk, owner, cash and competition, so you spend estimating time where you can win and make money.
items.x: In one sentence: every bid costs estimating time and every job uses crews, cash and bonding, so decide on purpose which ones to pursue, and walk away from the rest. A bid/no bid checklist Score each from 1 to 5: Question What to check Fit Is this the work and customer type you target? See choosing your market Capacity Crews, foremen and equipment available when it runs? Bonding and cash Within limits? What does the first 90 days of cash look like? Owner / GC How do they pay and treat contractors? Risk Unusual terms, liquidated damages, schedule, site conditions, design quality Competition How many bidders usually, and how close? Margin Realistic margin after overhead? Set a minimum score; below it, don't bid. Red flags Contract terms that shift design risk or unlimited damages to you. A schedule that can't be met with your crews. An owner or GC known for slow payment or disputes. A scope far outside your experience. Bidding only to keep the crew busy at a loss. Saying no well Thank the GC or owner, say you're not able to bid this one, and ask to stay on their list. A clear no is better than a weak bid. PM notes Track your hit rate by customer and job type. If you win 1 in 20 with a GC, your estimating time is better spent elsewhere.

items.t: Contracts and subcontracts: clauses to read before you sign
items.s: Scope, payment, pay-when-paid, indemnity, insurance, schedule and damages, changes, disputes and termination: what to look for and when to ask a lawyer.
items.x: In one sentence: the contract decides who carries which risk, so read the clauses that move money and liability before you sign, and get legal advice on the ones you don't understand. Clauses to read every time Clause What to look for Scope Plans, specs and addenda listed; your exclusions attached Price and payment Billing dates, retention, how long to pay Pay when paid / pay if paid Whether you get paid only if the GC is paid; California law limits pay if paid clauses Indemnity How far you must defend and pay for others' claims; California limits some forms Insurance Limits, additional insured, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory Schedule and damages Liquidated damages, delay damages, and whether you get time for others' delays Changes Who can order changes, notice deadlines, how they're priced Disputes Notice, claims process, mediation, arbitration, venue Termination For cause and for convenience; what you're paid Flow down Which prime contract terms pass to you; get a copy of the prime contract Public works On public jobs, many terms come from statute and the agency's standard specifications, and some subcontract clauses are limited by California law. See public works basics and public works claims. Your own subcontracts When you hire subs, use a written subcontract template reviewed by an attorney, with scope, insurance, schedule, safety, payment and change terms. A written subcontract with a licensed sub is also one of the conditions for treating them as a subcontractor. See california employment basics. Negotiating Mark up what you can't accept and explain why. Many GCs accept reasonable changes to indemnity, insurance or damages when asked. PM notes Make a one page summary of each contract (dates, notice deadlines, retention, damages, insurance) and give it to the PM and the foreman.

items.t: Project management basics for a small company
items.s: Who does what from award to closeout when the company has only a few people, and the weekly routine that keeps jobs on track.
items.x: In one sentence: in a small company the owner, the PM and the foreman share project management, so write down who owns each task and keep a short weekly routine. Who owns what Task Usually owned by Contract, insurance, bonds Owner / office Job start meeting, budget, schedule PM, with the foreman Submittals, RFIs, orders PM Daily work, crew, safety, daily reports Foreman Hours and cost codes Foreman, checked by the PM Change orders and notices PM, with the foreman's facts Billing PM and office Closeout PM, foreman and office The job start meeting Before work starts, the PM and foreman review scope, estimate (hours and quantities by cost code), schedule, long lead material, risks, safety plan and who the owner's contacts are. The weekly routine Monday: two week look ahead with each foreman: work, crew, material, equipment, inspections. Midweek: submittals, RFIs and orders reviewed; open items chased. Friday: hours checked against cost codes; changes and problems logged; next week planned. Every two weeks: job cost review. See job costing. Monthly: billing, cash forecast, WIP update. Tools A shared job folder, a submittal and RFI log, a change log and a two week schedule are enough to start. Field apps help once the routine exists. See pm day to day. PM notes Most job problems are visible two weeks ahead in the look ahead. The routine's job is to look.

items.s: Using utilization and true ownership cost to decide when to own equipment, and how to charge equipment to jobs.
items.x: In one sentence: buy equipment you'll use most working days for years, rent what you use occasionally, and charge every machine to the jobs that use it at a rate that covers what it really costs to own. The true cost of owning Purchase price and financing cost; depreciation (value lost each year); insurance, registration, taxes; maintenance and repairs; storage, transport, downtime. Divide the yearly total by the hours or days you'll really use it. Compare that rate with the rental rate. Utilization decides Use Usually Most working days, for years Own (cash, loan or finance lease) Steady for one long job Long term rental or operating lease A few days a month Rent Specialized, rarely used Rent with operator, or subcontract Charging equipment to jobs Set an internal rate for each owned machine (hourly or daily) that recovers its ownership and operating cost, and charge it to jobs like labor. Otherwise jobs look more profitable than they are and the equipment cost hides in overhead. See job costing. Keeping it working A simple maintenance schedule and a record per machine (hours, service, repairs) prevent the breakdown that stops a crew. Track where each machine is. Financing See credit lines and equipment finance. PM notes Idle equipment in the yard still costs money every month. Review utilization yearly and sell what you don't use.

items.t: Getting paid on change orders and closeout
items.s: Notice, documentation and pricing that get change orders signed, and a closeout routine that releases retention without months of chasing.
items.x: In one sentence: extra work and retention are often the profit on a job, and they get paid when you give notice on time, document as you go and close out completely. Change orders 1. Recognize extra work: the foreman knows the contract scope well enough to spot it. 2. Notify in writing within the contract's deadline, before doing the work when possible. 3. Document: daily reports, photos, hours and material by a separate cost code. 4. Price with backup: labor, burden, material, equipment, subs, overhead and profit as the contract allows. 5. Get it signed before or as the work is done; if not, keep tracking costs and follow the contract's claim process. 6. Bill approved changes on the next pay application. See change orders and public works claims. Closeout Start closeout before the work ends: punch list walked and worked; see acceptance testing punch list; as builts, O&M manuals, warranties, test reports; see closeout package; final quantities agreed; lien or payment releases exchanged with subs and suppliers; final billing and retention request. On public works, retention release follows statute and the agency's acceptance; see progress payments retention and public works closeout. Tracking Keep a list of every open change and every job in closeout, with amount, status and next action, and review it every week. PM notes An unsigned change order is an unbilled invoice. Treat the change log like accounts receivable.

items.s: What changes when a specialty subcontractor starts bidding as the prime: bonding, coordination, paperwork, risk, and how to make the step gradually.
items.x: In one sentence: as a prime you hold the owner's contract, the bonds and the coordination of every sub, so step up on jobs where your own trade is most of the work. What changes Topic As a sub As a prime Contract With a GC With the owner or agency Bonds Sometimes Bid, performance and payment bonds, usually Coordination Your scope All trades, traffic control, testing, schedule Paperwork Your submittals and payroll Everyone's: submittals, RFIs, certified payroll, DBE, closeout Payment From the GC From the owner; you pay the subs Risk Your scope The whole job, including your subs' failures Where specialty primes win Agencies often advertise work where one trade is most of the scope: on Caltrans, electrical jobs like lighting, signals, ramp metering and communications are bid with an electrical contractor as prime. See what a caltrans electrical contractor does. Making the step gradually 1. Start with small jobs within your trade where the other trades are minor. 2. Build relationships with reliable subs (traffic control, paving, striping, civil). 3. Line up bonding before you bid. See bonding capacity. 4. Add the office capacity for prime paperwork: submittals, RFIs, certified payroll, DBE, subcontractor listing. See subcontractor listing and dbe requirements. 5. Learn from each job's closeout before bidding bigger. PM notes Your subs' performance becomes yours. Choose them on reliability, insurance and payroll compliance, not just price.

items.t: When to hire your first PM, estimator or office manager
items.s: The signs that the owner has become the bottleneck, which role to hire first, and how to hand over work without losing control.
items.x: In one sentence: hire your first office role when the owner's time, not the work available, limits the company, and pick the role that frees the owner from what they do least well. Signs it's time Bids are missed or rushed because there's no time to estimate. Billing is late, change orders unsigned, paperwork piling up. The owner works in the office at night after a day in the field. Jobs lose money because no one watches cost during the job. Which role first Bottleneck First hire Not enough bids, or rushed ones Estimator Jobs running without follow up: submittals, RFIs, changes, cost Project manager Billing, payroll, compliance, insurance, files Office manager / administrator Many small contractors start with an office manager, because it frees the owner and gets cash in faster, then a PM. Handing over work Write down how you do the task today, even roughly. Hand over a whole responsibility, not random tasks. Agree on decisions they can make alone and those they bring to you. Review weekly at first, then less often. Paying for it The new role must be paid by more work, faster cash or better margins. Estimate which and by how much before hiring, and check after six months. See overhead and markup. PM notes The owner's job changes from doing the work to checking it and finding more of it. That change is harder than the hire.

items.t: Systems before growth: software, processes and a company handbook
items.s: The few written processes and tools a small contractor needs before adding crews and jobs, so quality and cash don't fall apart as the company grows.
items.x: In one sentence: growth multiplies whatever you do today, good or bad, so write down how the company works and put simple systems in place before adding crews and jobs. Write down the key processes One page each, in plain words: bid/no bid and estimating; see when to pass on a job; job start meeting; see project management small company; daily report, time and cost codes; purchasing and receiving material; change orders and notices; see getting paid on changes and closeout; billing and collections; hiring and onboarding; see hiring field crews; safety program; see safety program; closeout. The company handbook Policies employees need: pay, hours and breaks, time keeping, vehicles and tools, phones, safety rules, drug and alcohol policy, discipline, leave. Have an employment attorney review it. See california employment basics. Tools Accounting with job costing. Payroll that handles California and certified payroll. A field app for daily reports, time, photos and material requests. A shared document system with a standard job folder. Choose tools after the process is written; software doesn't fix a process no one agreed on. See procore for small gc for how to judge a larger platform. Numbers to watch every month Backlog, revenue, gross margin by job, overhead, cash forecast, receivables aging, WIP over/under billing, safety (meetings held, incidents), bid hit rate. PM notes If the owner took a two week vacation, would jobs, billing and payroll keep running? That's the test of the systems.
